Chris Van Hollen launches bid to unseat Schumer as Senate majority leader

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) announced Thursday night that he would challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) for Senate majority leader, citing a need for new leadership to address economic issues and political corruption. Van Hollen framed his bid as a response to voter demands for change. Meanwhile, Mother Jones highlighted the economic challenges facing Democrats, including inflation and the impact of Trump's policies, suggesting that addressing these issues is crucial for the party's success. The Intercept reported that Democrats in the House failed to pass an impeachment resolution against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, with several Democrats citing traffic as a reason for their absence.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both report that Van Hollen is challenging Schumer for Senate majority leader, but the Examiner emphasizes Van Hollen's call for new leadership to address economic issues, while FOX News notes Van Hollen's acknowledgment of being an "underdog" and his support from progressive figures like Bernie Sanders. The Intercept and Mother Jones do not mention Van Hollen's leadership bid, focusing instead on internal Democratic struggles and economic policy discussions. The Intercept attributes the failure of the impeachment vote to traffic and other logistical issues, while Mother Jones does not mention the impeachment vote at all.

Sources Washington Examiner · Mother Jones · The Intercept · NPR · Axios · FOX News

Duffy, Mullin call for $50B air travel 'overhaul' in fiery ground stop briefing

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all U.S. flights for nearly four hours on Friday due to a communications issue, according to multiple accounts. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a briefing after the FAA lifted the ground stop, calling for $50 billion in funding to overhaul the nation’s air traffic control system. Duffy stated the system is “incredibly old” and that the outage was caused by overloaded routers leading to inconsistent data. Mullin emphasized there is “zero evidence” of a cyber-attack and that the situation is a telecommunications outage. The FAA confirmed the airspace was reopened at around 8:15 p.m. EST, though normal operations are expected to take time to resume.

The ground stop, the second such event since the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks, affected over 10,218 flights, with more than 3,000 canceled, according to FlightAware. The FAA cited “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” for the ground stop. Some college football games were impacted, with teams scrambling to adjust travel plans, including switching to buses or altering kickoff times. The situation caused widespread chaos, with passengers stranded and airports in disarray.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and The Guardian both state the FAA issued the ground stop at around 4 p.m. EST, while Just The News reports it was issued at 3:36 p.m. EST. The Hill and The Guardian mention the FAA’s SMART program as an AI tool, while The Guardian and Just The News note that the outage was not connected to this system. The Hill and The Guardian report the ground stop lasted nearly four hours, while Just The News states it was the second such event since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. The Hill and The Guardian mention the last widespread stoppage was in 2023 due to a contractor outage, while Just The News refers to the 2023 incident as a pilot notification system issue. The Hill and The Guardian report the ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. EST, while Just The News states the FAA confirmed the airspace was open at that time. The Hill and The Guardian mention the FAA’s last widespread stoppage was on Sept. 11, 2001, while Just The News refers to it as a ground stop issued for the 9/11 terror attacks.

Sources The Hill · Newsweek · NPR · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · Just The News

All passengers and crew accounted for after New Orleans boat crash in ‘miracle on the Mississippi’

A tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon, resulting in 32 people being taken to local hospitals. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno described the incident as a “miracle on the Mississippi,” noting that no one was killed or critically injured. The American Heritage, operated by American Cruise Lines, was struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker, which had lost control. The cruise ship eventually rolled onto its side, with some passengers and crew ending up in the river. Rescue efforts by multiple agencies, including the Coast Guard and Harbor Police, were credited with ensuring all individuals were accounted for.

The American Heritage had 197 passengers onboard when it was hit, according to Port of New Orleans press secretary Kimberly Curth. About two hours before the collision, the ship had docked to begin passenger disembarkation. Officials confirmed that the tanker lost steering control, though the exact cause remains under investigation. Video footage from the scene showed the tanker T-boning the side of the cruise ship, leading to the vessel rolling over. Witnesses described the event as surreal, with some people in the water and others on the remaining part of the ship.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that the American Heritage had 197 passengers onboard when it was hit, while The Daily Wire and Just The News state the number was 129. The Guardian and CBS News also mention that 32 people were hospitalized, with none in critical condition, while The Daily Wire and Just The News report the same. FOX News and Axios both mention that the exact cause of the crash is under investigation, with the Coast Guard citing a loss of steering. The Guardian and CBS News provide more detail about the sequence of events, including the tanker’s path and the video footage obtained from Mardi Gras World. The Daily Wire and Just The News do not mention the video footage or the tanker’s path. The Guardian and CBS News also note that the American Heritage rolled onto its side, while The Daily Wire and Just The News do not specify the exact position of the ship after the collision.

Sources The Guardian · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Just The News · Axios · CBS News

Mississippi Couldn’t Stop Scott Colom’s Victory—But It Wasn’t for a Lack of Trying

Democrat Scott Colom won the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, defeating Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 4,600 votes. Colom, the first elected Black senator from Mississippi in over 150 years, will be sworn in next year. The race, which took over a week to call, highlighted the state’s archaic voting system and the legal challenges that followed. Election officials will finalize remaining affidavit ballots, which were affected by a voter roll purge. Both campaigns are preparing for potential legal action, as Mississippi does not have laws for automatic vote recounts or runoff elections. Hyde-Smith’s campaign demanded that counties separate affidavit ballots from regular and absentee ballots, a move similar to one the Trump administration made in California.

Where the accounts differ

Slate and ABC News both note that Hyde-Smith’s campaign demanded counties separate affidavit ballots, but Slate attributes this to Mississippi law, while ABC News does not specify the legal basis. Axios and BBC both mention the historical significance of Colom’s win, but Axios provides specific county-by-county vote totals, while BBC focuses on the emotional impact and grassroots efforts. The Nation highlights the historical context by comparing Colom’s win to Hiram Revels’ 1870 election, a detail not included in the other accounts. NPR mentions the White House warning Democrats about future investigations, a point absent in the other outlets.

Sources Slate · Axios · The Nation · NPR · ABC News · BBC

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China

U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin are set to hold an unprecedented three-way meeting next week on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. The White House confirmed the meeting, which will focus on nuclear arms control and the Iran war, though no agreement is expected. Trump plans to avoid discussing Russia’s war in Ukraine during the meeting. Elon Musk will travel with Trump to China but will not attend the meeting. The summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 Yalta Conference, though Russian officials have dismissed the parallel.

The meeting will be the first trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia. Trump is expected to discuss nuclear stockpiles and the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but not Ukraine. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) between the U.S. and Russia expired in February, and Trump has rejected Russia’s proposal to extend it, demanding a new deal that includes China. The White House has described the meeting as the start of a conversation rather than a negotiation.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and ABC News both report that Trump will not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the meeting. BBC and Christian Science Monitor also state that Ukraine is not on the agenda, while Just The News and New York Post mention the war in Iran as a topic. Al Jazeera and ABC News note that Musk will not attend the meeting, while New York Post adds that Musk will travel with Trump. Just The News and New York Post mention the trade agreement with China, while Al Jazeera and ABC News do not. The New York Post reports that Trump will discuss North Korea, which is not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Al Jazeera · ABC News · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · Just The News · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeats Republican Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District

Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert lost her re-election bid in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher, according to the Associated Press. The race was extremely close, with Laubacher securing 48.8% of the vote compared to Boebert’s 47.9%, as 99% of ballots were counted. Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris received 3.3% of the vote. Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, previously served on the Biden administration’s National Security Council. Boebert, who represented the district since 2024, was running for her fourth term in the House. The race marks another Democratic flip in a Republican stronghold, contributing to Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress. Laubacher’s victory follows a broader trend of Republican losses in midterm elections, with Democrats now holding 256 seats in the House compared to Republicans’ 169.

Laubacher, who moved to the district in 2024, ran as a common-sense candidate focused on affordability, ending corruption, and improving rural healthcare. She previously served as a Republican and later switched parties, citing dissatisfaction with the GOP. Boebert, a vocal Trump ally, faced multiple controversies during her tenure, including allegations of inappropriate conduct, ethics complaints, and comments about the 2020 election. Despite these issues, she occasionally criticized Trump, such as when she supported a bill to release the Epstein files, which led to Trump calling her a “carpetbagger” and “dumb.”

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and The Daily Caller both mention that Boebert moved to the 4th district in 2024 to avoid a close race, while The Guardian and CBS News describe her move as part of a broader pattern of controversy and political maneuvering. The Guardian and CBS News also note that Laubacher changed her party affiliation in 2025, a detail not included in FOX News or The Daily Caller. The Daily Caller and The New York Post report that Boebert’s campaign lawyer claimed “unusual voting patterns” and expected a recount, which is not mentioned in other accounts. The Guardian and CBS News provide more detail on Boebert’s personal controversies, including her divorce, public apology, and ethics complaint, which are omitted or briefly mentioned in other outlets.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · CBS News · Just The News · New York Post · The Daily Caller

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. He will replace outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who has been in office since 2018. Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, will be the youngest governor in state history. The race was conducted under Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, which requires a majority of votes to win. Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. The state’s last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002. The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes, including those from remote areas. A separate AP race call indicated that a ballot measure to scrap the ranked-choice system failed, keeping it in place.

Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign. He emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and described himself as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski. The state faces challenges including rising costs, flat state funding, and a looming natural gas shortage. Voters have also been migrating out of the state for over a decade.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and Newsweek both state that Kreiss-Tomkins won with over 50 percent of the vote, avoiding a ranked-choice runoff. However, Newsweek reports that Kreiss-Tomkins secured 50.8 percent of the vote, while NPR does not specify the exact percentage. CBS News and the New York Post do not mention the exact vote share, though CBS notes that the AP called the race. The New York Post states that Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August’s open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. NPR and Newsweek do not mention Begich’s withdrawal. The New York Post also notes that Trump endorsed Bernadette Wilson, while Newsweek and CBS do not specify which candidates Trump endorsed. NPR and Newsweek both mention that the ranked-choice system was kept in place, but NPR adds that the measure to scrap it failed, while Newsweek does not.

Sources NPR · New York Post · Newsweek · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Ex-CIA Director John Brennan’s Son Arrested On Child Porn Charges

The son of former CIA Director John Brennan, Kyle Brennan, was arrested by the FBI on child pornography charges. The arrest occurred in the Eastern District of Virginia, where Kyle, 40, was charged with knowingly transporting child pornography using a means or facility of interstate or foreign commerce. Federal agents reportedly seized and searched Kyle’s cellular phone, finding nearly 90 images of child sex abuse material, including a photo of a “fully nude pubescent minor girl on a locker bench.” The FBI executed a search warrant on his phone, which allegedly contained “sexually explicit” materials of children. The case originated from Adobe CyberTipline reports that flagged accounts linked to Brennan for uploading illicit files involving minors.

The FBI’s investigation led to the identification of an IP address registered to Kyle Brennan at an address in Warrenton, Virginia. According to court documents, the FBI found approximately 88 images on his phone that appeared to depict minor girls, including prepubescent girls engaged in sexually explicit conduct. One image was described as a “morphed image” combining the face of a minor girl with the naked body of another, and was later identified as a 12-year-old girl. The FBI also searched Brennan’s residence and devices in the summer of 2024, referring the case to the FBI in October 2026.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Caller and The Federalist both mention that the FBI seized and searched Brennan’s phone, but only The Daily Caller attributes this to the Daily Mail. The Federalist states that the phone contained “approximately 88 images,” while The Daily Caller and Just The News report “nearly 90 images.” The Federalist and FOX News describe the image of a “fully nude, pubescent minor girl on a locker bench” with her wrists and ankles bound and mouth gagged, a detail not included in The Daily Caller or Just The News. The Federalist and FOX News also note that the FBI searched Brennan’s residence in the summer of 2024, a detail not mentioned in The Daily Caller or Just The News.

Sources The Daily Caller · The Federalist · Just The News · Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled center or lean-left or left covered this story.

Israel Used a U.S.-Made Missile to Kill Six at Gaza’s Nasser Hospital

The Israeli airstrike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, Gaza, killed six people, including surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaaira, and wounded 52 others, according to Gaza health officials and Médecins Sans Frontières. The attack occurred on Wednesday evening, with victims including a disabled man and a patient of Abu Shaaira. The hospital’s emergency, surgery, radiology, and laboratory departments were closed following the strike, which damaged multiple floors and caused structural collapse in some areas. The Israeli military claimed it targeted a Hamas commander, though it did not provide evidence. The attack is the fourth on a hospital since the so-called ceasefire agreement in October 2025 and the seventh on the Nasser complex, including a double-tap strike in August 2025.

The strike occurred during a time when surgical patients were waiting for operations, according to Dr. Ayman Abu Ubaid, a wounded surgeon at the hospital. He described the attack as sudden and devastating, with thick smoke, fires, and casualties. The hospital director, Dr. Ahmed al-Fara, noted that Nasser Hospital is one of the last functioning healthcare facilities in Gaza, having been attacked seven times since the war began. The hospital has also been damaged in previous strikes, including one that killed five journalists in a double-tap attack last year.

Where the accounts differ

The Intercept reports that the Israeli military used a U.S.-made GBU-39/B missile, manufactured by Boeing, in the attack, and that the strike was the fourth on a hospital since the October 2025 ceasefire. It also mentions that the attack was the seventh on the Nasser complex, including a double-tap strike in August 2025. The Intercept attributes the claim about the U.S.-made missile to Feroze Sidhwa, who described it as active participation in the murder of healthcare workers. The Guardian does not mention the missile type or its manufacturer, nor does it reference the October 2025 ceasefire or the August 2025 double-tap strike. The Guardian also includes details about Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, a patient killed in the strike, which The Intercept does not mention.

Sources The Intercept · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader

Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday that he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Van Hollen argued that the American people called for change from the status quo that isn't working for working people. Schumer responded by stating he has the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader. The leadership race is set for a secret ballot in December, with Van Hollen's bid highlighting growing divisions within the Democratic Party.

Van Hollen's challenge comes amid a broader push for change within the party, with progressive Democrats arguing that Schumer's leadership has failed to address key issues like affordability and war. The party's midterm election success has led to calls for new leadership, with some senators-elect, including Abdul El-Sayed, publicly rejecting Schumer's leadership. The race is expected to be closely contested, with Van Hollen claiming he has more than 10 senators on his side.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Democrats need to change leadership to deliver on an agenda focused on affordability and change, and that Schumer should step aside for younger members. It attributes calls for change to voters and criticizes the party's ties to donors and groups like AIPAC. The article does not mention Van Hollen's challenge or any leadership election.

The Guardian and Washington Examiner both report that Van Hollen announced his bid to challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader, with the Guardian noting that Schumer responded by stating he has the votes to continue as leader. The Guardian also mentions that the race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades, while the Washington Examiner emphasizes Van Hollen's call for new leadership to address an economy rigged against working people.

Sources Al Jazeera · Axios · FOX News · The Nation · Washington Examiner · The Guardian

Brooklyn building collapse kills at least two children and six adults, injuring 18

A three-storey residential building in Brooklyn, New York, collapsed into an adjacent construction site on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and injuring 18. Rescue efforts continued through Thursday as crews searched for survivors. The FDNY reported that six people were found dead at the scene, with two more dying later from their injuries. Among the deceased were two children and four construction workers from a nearby site. The collapse occurred around 4pm on Flatbush Avenue, and the search-and-rescue operation involved over 250 first responders. Officials described the conditions as extremely dangerous, with heavy rain expected to complicate efforts. The building, which housed apartments, was partially destroyed, exposing interior spaces like bedrooms and wardrobes. The New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, expressed heartbreak over the tragedy and urged the public to stay away from the site.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that the death toll rose to eight, while FOX News and Just The News state at least two people were killed initially, with the final toll not confirmed until Thursday. The Guardian and CBS News mention that two children were among the deceased, while FOX News and Just The News do not specify the ages of the victims. The Guardian and CBS News report that six people were found dead at the scene, with two more dying later, while FOX News and Just The News do not provide this detail. The Guardian and CBS News state that four firefighters were injured, while FOX News and Just The News report that one firefighter was injured. The Guardian and CBS News mention that the building housed a number of apartments, while FOX News and Just The News do not specify the building's use. The Guardian and CBS News report that the FDNY completed its search by 3:37pm on Thursday, while FOX News and Just The News do not provide this time.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · The Daily Wire · CBS News · FOX News · Just The News

Pete Hegseth’s Crew Got Chewed Out at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his entourage were reprimanded by a military sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. The incident occurred after Hegseth and his staff, including his wife Jennifer and several aides, posed for photos in front of the tomb. Loud laughter and chatter from the group prompted the sentinel to issue a sharp rebuke, shouting, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed the event, stating the department honors the sacrifices of military personnel. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a sacred war memorial, has been guarded by the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, since 1948. The sentinel’s role includes maintaining decorum and preventing disrespectful behavior at the site.

Hegseth later awarded a medal to the soldier who reprimanded his group. According to CBS News and the New York Post, Hegseth posted photos of himself pinning a Joint Service Commendation Medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias, a member of the Old Guard. The Pentagon confirmed the award, noting Iglesias was recognized for his duties at the tomb. The incident has drawn attention to Hegseth’s recent survival of impeachment proceedings and his controversial policies regarding military personnel.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Hill report that Hegseth was accompanied by his wife and senior staff, while FOX News and the New York Post specify the names of some aides present, including Ricky Buria, Patrick Weaver, and Tami Radabaugh. CBS News and the New York Post mention that Hegseth awarded a medal to Iglesias, while Mother Jones and The Hill do not mention any award. The Hill and FOX News include details about Trump’s presence and his reaction to the incident, which are omitted in Mother Jones and CBS News. The New York Post and CBS News attribute the award to Hegseth, while Mother Jones and The Hill do not specify who awarded the medal.

Sources Mother Jones · CBS News · BBC · The Hill · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US doctor kills building manager after long-running dispute over mould, police say

A doctor who had been in an ongoing dispute over mould and other issues at his Washington DC apartment fatally shot his building's manager and fired at four others before killing himself, police say. Building manager James Stuart, 46, was pronounced dead at the scene, while four others were rushed to local hospitals for treatment. The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House. Police said the suspect, identified as 55-year-old doctor Matt Wade Lambert, then barricaded himself in an apartment, and later died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. While the suspect was barricaded, "he did fire through the door at officers at least on two occasions", Jefferey Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, said at a news conference.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and FOX News both report that the suspect had a legal dispute with the condo association over maintenance issues and mold, but FOX News adds that the dispute had previously resulted in a civil lawsuit filed by Lambert. The Daily Wire and Axios do not mention the lawsuit. FOX News also states that Lambert severed a natural gas line to a fireplace and sparked a fire, which was contained by the building’s sprinkler system, while BBC and The Daily Wire do not mention this. The Washington Examiner and New York Post both identify the victim as James Stuart, the building manager, but the New York Post adds that Lambert had a feud over black mold in his $1.1 million apartment. The Daily Wire and Axios do not specify the nature of the dispute beyond a "conflict" with the homeowners association.

Sources BBC · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Axios

White House Warns Democrats of Criminal Investigations for Investigating Trump

The White House has issued a warning to incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) that discussing investigations into the Trump administration could be considered criminal. White House Counsel Will Scharf wrote to Garcia, stating that Congress must have a legitimate legislative purpose for its investigative acts, or it constitutes an abuse of power. Scharf cited social media posts from lawmakers, including Rep. Analilia Mejia, who tweeted, “We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads.” The letter echoes President Trump’s claims that Democrats are engaging in “extortion at the highest level” and should be held accountable. In response, Garcia stated that Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House.

Attorney General Todd Blanche clarified that the Justice Department has no active criminal investigations into Democratic lawmakers’ remarks about their plans to scrutinize the Trump administration. Blanche said he has not seen any statements that crossed a criminal line. Meanwhile, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer warned that focusing too much on corruption could distract lawmakers from delivering on what Americans voted for.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and NPR both report that White House Counsel Will Scharf wrote to Rep. Robert Garcia, warning that investigations could be criminal. However, Mother Jones includes specific quotes from Garcia and Mejia, while NPR attributes the quotes to social media posts and does not include the exact wording. The Washington Examiner and New York Post report that Attorney General Todd Blanche stated there are no ongoing criminal investigations into Democratic lawmakers’ remarks, while Just The News and The Daily Wire do not mention Blanche’s clarification. The New York Post and The Daily Wire also report that Sen. Richard Blumenthal is targeting donors to the White House ballroom, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · NPR · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Just The News · The Daily Wire

Trump redirects Vance from Iran to focus on combatting fraud in Democratic-led states

President Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus from Iran negotiations to addressing alleged corruption in Democratic-led states. Trump claimed the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran, stating the country has "their money" and "their Strait." Vance, who has been involved in diplomatic efforts with Iran, including a failed June memorandum of understanding, is now being tasked with investigating fraud in states like California, Illinois, and Minnesota. The directive came amid Republican losses in the midterm elections, which Trump and Vance have both linked to the ongoing war with Iran.

Vance, who chairs the administration's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, has been a vocal critic of the war with Iran. He previously questioned whether the conflict was worth the political and economic costs, suggesting it contributed to the Republicans' losses. Trump's message on Truth Social emphasized the need to focus on "Massive Corruption and Crime" in Democrat-run areas, framing the issue as a priority for the administration.

Where the accounts differ

NPR does not mention the specific states targeted by Trump or the claim about "their money" and "their Strait." Al Jazeera and Axios both include the list of states (California, Illinois, Minnesota) and the claim about Iran's financial assets. The Daily Wire adds the phrase "Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," which is not present in the other accounts. Just The News provides more detail about the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, including the involvement of multiple federal agencies and specific cases like the Minnesota Medicaid fraud. New York Post notes that Vance is not entirely off the Iran portfolio and could return if there is progress in talks, a point not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · Axios · Just The News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

Microsoft Outage Disrupts Email, Workplace Apps

A Microsoft 365 outage disrupted access to email and workplace applications Thursday as the company worked to restore service. Outage tracker Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems Thursday afternoon. Thousands of reports also involved Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 services. Microsoft was still working to restore affected servers just after 4:30 p.m. ET, when it said it was also considering reversing recent configuration updates to speed recovery. The company acknowledged problems accessing Exchange Online, its cloud email service, shortly before 1 p.m. ET.

The outage impacted a wide range of services, including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, with reports from users in 74 countries. The disruption continued into Friday, with some services still experiencing issues. Microsoft said it was working to improve server stability and traffic flow, but service health remained variable. The company also mentioned that it was extending the "email timeout window" to 48 hours to help protect delayed messages during recovery.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Guardian both mention Microsoft's initial explanation of elevated load on part of its infrastructure, while Al Jazeera and CBS News note that the elevated load was not caused by an increase in traffic. The Guardian and Al Jazeera report that Microsoft determined some servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, while The Daily Wire and ABC News state that Microsoft paused deployments and redirected traffic as part of its recovery efforts. Newsweek provides additional context on the impact of the outage, including disruptions to government services, airlines, and visa processing, which are not detailed in the other accounts. The Guardian and Al Jazeera mention the outage affecting more than 430 million Microsoft 365 users, while The Daily Wire and CBS News cite 130,000 reports of Outlook problems.

Sources The Daily Wire · Newsweek · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · ABC News · CBS News

GOP holdouts complicate Trump’s final chances to reshape US courts

President Donald Trump is facing pushback from his own party as Republicans race to confirm as many of his judicial nominees as possible before Democrats take control of the Senate in January. The midterm losses left Republicans only weeks to fill lifetime seats on the federal bench while they still have the votes. Making matters worse for the president’s nominations agenda, Sens. Thom Tillis (R-NC) and John Cornyn (R-TX) helped force Trump to withdraw an Arkansas appeals court nominee Tuesday, and Tillis says he’ll vote against other nominees if a Republican senator from their home state objects.

Senate Republicans are racing to confirm President Donald Trump’s judicial nominees before Democrats take control of the chamber in January, seeking to fill as many federal court vacancies as possible while they still have the votes. Republicans have already confirmed 56 Article III judges during Trump’s second term, according to the Senate Republican Conference, which highlighted the confirmations Thursday. GOP leaders hope to confirm as many as 25 more nominees before the new Congress convenes, including four appeals court nominees and 21 district court picks.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire differ on the number of judges confirmed and the number of nominees Republicans hope to confirm. The Washington Examiner does not mention the 56 confirmed judges or the goal of confirming 25 more nominees. The Daily Wire also reports that some Democrats supported Trump’s nominees, which the Washington Examiner does not mention. The Daily Caller and The Federalist do not discuss the judicial confirmation process at all, focusing instead on internal GOP dynamics and the impact of the midterms on party leadership. The New York Post and CBS News focus on House leadership changes and the threat of Democratic investigations, which are not covered in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Federalist · New York Post · CBS News

No source labeled center covered this story.

The brief ends here.

House GOP selects Jim Jordan as new leader amid internal divisions

House Republicans have chosen Jim Jordan, a hardline member of the House Freedom Caucus, as their new leader following a contentious vote. Jordan defeated longtime leader Steve Scalise in a 106–73 race, signaling a shift toward a more confrontational approach. Jordan has positioned himself as a fighter capable of defending President Trump against Democratic investigations and reclaiming congressional power. Some Republicans, like Rep. Randy Fine and Dan Meuser, have endorsed Jordan's aggressive stance, arguing that the party needs a strong leader after a significant midterm defeat. Others, including Rep. Carlos Gimenez, have questioned whether the party's losses were due to policy failures, particularly regarding immigration, and whether Jordan is the right choice to lead the charge back to power.

Separately, Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorization and of directing extrajudicial killings. The impeachment effort failed in a 211–204 vote, with all Republicans except Massie voting to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee. Hegseth called the effort a "farce" and "sabotage," while Massie argued the impeachment was about upholding the rule of law.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and NPR both report that Jordan's victory marks a shift in GOP leadership dynamics, but Axios adds that Jordan's rise could sharpen tensions with Senate Republicans, while NPR focuses on Jordan's reputation as a brawler and his experience in Trump-era battles. The Free Press and Slate both discuss the impeachment of Hegseth, but the Free Press highlights the potential long-term impact of the impeachment threat, while Slate emphasizes the legal and historical significance of the charges. Axios and BBC both note the impeachment vote, but Axios provides more detail on the internal GOP divisions, while BBC focuses on the political implications for the upcoming congressional term.

Sources Axios · BBC · The Free Press · Slate · Mother Jones · NPR

Mississippi, Once the Epicenter of Jim Crow, Elects Its First Black Senator Since Reconstruction

Scott Colom, a Mississippi Democratic Senate candidate, won a narrow victory in the state's Senate race, becoming the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. Colom, a longtime district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by less than 5,000 votes. The race was marked by a razor-thin margin, with the final count showing Colom with approximately 49.2% of the vote compared to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%. The outcome was confirmed by multiple outlets after a week of vote counting. Colom’s victory is seen as a historic moment for Mississippi, which has a long history of racial violence and segregation, including the lynching of Emmett Till and the assassination of Medgar Evers.

Colom ran on a platform focused on healthcare access, rural hospital preservation, and affordability. His campaign emphasized bipartisanship, noting that many Mississippians support policies that benefit all residents regardless of political affiliation. The race was also influenced by national political developments, including the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which weakened the Voting Rights Act and spurred increased voter turnout among Black communities. Mississippi Republican Gov. Tate Reeves had previously called for legislative action to remove Rep. Bennie Thompson, the only Black member of Congress from the state, but Colom’s victory has sparked widespread celebration and reflection on the state’s civil rights history.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and BBC both note that Colom’s victory is the first for a Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, but BBC adds that it would be the first in over 140 years. NPR and New York Post describe the race as a "nailbiter" with a margin of less than 5,000 votes, while Mother Jones and BBC mention the final margin as less than 1% and 2,500 ballots respectively. The New York Post states that Colom received 49.2% of the vote, while Mother Jones and BBC do not specify exact percentages. FOX News and Washington Examiner do not cover the race in detail, focusing instead on other election outcomes. The New York Post mentions that Colom became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982, while Mother Jones and BBC do not specify the year of the previous Democratic Senate win.

Sources Mother Jones · NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post

Republicans and Democrats react to Nvidia CEO's alleged affair with Chinese spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faced scrutiny after allegations emerged that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a woman U.S. officials believe was a Chinese intelligence asset. The affair, which Huang admitted to, has raised concerns about national security and corporate espionage. The FBI and Justice Department are investigating whether Huang's relationship compromised U.S. interests or corporate trade secrets. The scandal has intensified debates over U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips to China, with lawmakers pushing for tighter restrictions. Senate Republicans, including Sen. John Kennedy, called for a full investigation into the allegations, while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries supported new legislation to restrict China's access to U.S. technology.

The scandal has also drawn attention to the role of corporate leadership in national security. The White House, under President Donald Trump, has expressed support for Huang, with Trump claiming he called Huang to check on his well-being. Trump has previously praised Huang for his contributions to U.S. tech and AI development, including during a White House summit where he called Nvidia chips "the backbone of frontier superintelligence."

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Hill both report that Sen. John Kennedy said he "lost my breath" upon learning of the allegations, while The Daily Wire and The Free Press focus on Huang's management style and the broader implications of the scandal. The Hill mentions that Jeffries and other lawmakers met with top administration officials, including Jay Clayton and John Ratcliffe, for a classified briefing, a detail not included in other accounts. The Newsweek article notes that Huang admitted to an affair but not with whom, while The Mother Jones article states that Huang confirmed the affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed. The Free Press and The Daily Wire provide more context on Huang's personal and professional life, which other accounts omit.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Hill · The Daily Wire · The Free Press · Newsweek · Mother Jones

Pete Hegseth’s Crew Got Chewed Out at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his wife, Jennifer, along with several members of his staff, were reprimanded by a U.S. Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. The incident occurred after the group, which included Hegseth and his aides, was seen laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the memorial. The sentinel shouted, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed the event, stating the department honors the sacrifices of military personnel. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a sacred war memorial, has been guarded by the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment since 1948. The sentinels are known for enforcing strict decorum at the site, often reprimanding visitors who disrupt the solemnity.

The event took place during a Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, which also included President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump. The group was reportedly reprimanded shortly after the ceremony, with the sentinel’s rebuke occurring as the group was departing the site. The exact moment of the laughter and who was involved remains unclear, though multiple accounts describe the incident as occurring after the group had finished taking photos.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and New York Post both mention that Hegseth’s group was reprimanded for laughter, while CBS News and BBC do not specify the cause of the reprimand, only that a group including Hegseth was reprimanded. FOX News adds that the incident occurred shortly after President Trump left the ceremony, and that the reprimand happened around 12:30 p.m. Mother Jones and New York Post also note that the sentinel’s rebuke was part of the group’s departure, while CBS News and BBC describe the reprimand as occurring after the group had finished taking photos. Additionally, Mother Jones and New York Post mention that the sentinel’s rebuke was part of the group’s departure, while CBS News and BBC describe the reprimand as occurring after the group had finished taking photos. FOX News and New York Post also note that the sentinel’s rebuke was part of the group’s departure, while CBS News and BBC describe the reprimand as occurring after the group had finished taking photos.

Sources Mother Jones · CBS News · BBC · FOX News · New York Post · Newsweek

Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Moscow to meet with Putin, discuss Ukraine peace talks

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, following two days of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. The meetings were the first such talks since February and included discussions on a prisoner exchange deal, security guarantees for Ukraine, and broader European security arrangements. Both sides acknowledged differences remain, particularly on territorial issues and post-war security. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to meet with the envoys in Dublin later on Thursday. Russia and Ukraine continued their long-range strike campaigns overnight, with Ukraine reporting intercepted drones and missiles.

The talks in Abu Dhabi resulted in an agreement on a major prisoner exchange, described as the largest of the war, though no significant breakthroughs were achieved on ending the conflict. U.S. officials expressed hope that the meeting would pave the way for further negotiations, including bringing European partners into the process. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is nearing its fifth anniversary, with both sides remaining far apart on key issues such as the fate of occupied territory and security guarantees.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that the prisoner exchange was described as the largest of the war and attributes the claim to Kushner. The Washington Examiner omits any mention of the prisoner exchange agreement, instead focusing on Russia’s unchanged war aims. Al Jazeera states that the prisoner exchange was agreed upon but notes that Kyiv has rejected Putin’s demands for surrendering Donbas. The Guardian reports that the prisoner exchange is expected to involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side, a detail not included in ABC News or Al Jazeera. NPR mentions the prisoner exchange but does not specify the number of prisoners involved. The New York Post highlights the prisoner exchange as a breakthrough but does not mention the number of prisoners.

Sources ABC News · Washington Examiner · Al Jazeera · NPR · New York Post · The Guardian

UK probes alleged Iran-backed plot against base hosting US forces

Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed. The indictment names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, who are alleged to have acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah. Prosecutors allege the men orchestrated attacks targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops, including an attempted attack on a London synagogue. The U.S. has designated both groups as foreign terrorist organizations.

The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot, with as many as seven attacks taking place there. The indictment describes an operation directed by the suspects from thousands of miles away, including real-time coordination via FaceTime. Al-Hassani allegedly coached an attacker through igniting and hurling incendiary devices and later directed another man to "light it up like a Christmas tree" during an attack on a London synagogue. The men allegedly prepared for an attack on RAF Fairford by acquiring vans, fuel, and chemical accelerants, with the vans disguised as fuel delivery and pool supply vehicles. British authorities seized the vans near the base and arrested those inside.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and BBC both state that the U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long-range bombing aircraft from RAF Fairford after the incident, while FOX News and The Daily Wire mention that approximately a dozen U.S. B-1 bombers were previously withdrawn from the base. NPR and BBC also note that the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks, whereas FOX News and The Daily Wire provide more specific details about the number of attacks and their locations. The New York Post and The Daily Wire mention that al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey and transferred to the U.S., while NPR and BBC do not specify the location of his arrest. The New York Post and The Daily Wire attribute the phrase "work" to al-Saadi as a reference to terrorist activity, while other accounts do not make this characterization.

Sources NPR · Axios · BBC · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Russian Ambassador to US Alexander Darchiev dies suddenly at 66

Alexander Darchiev, Russia’s ambassador to the United States, died suddenly on November 11, 2026, at the age of 66, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. The ministry announced his death without specifying a cause. Darchiev was appointed as ambassador in March 2025 and had previously served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021. He was known for his role in high-stakes diplomatic negotiations, including prisoner swaps involving Americans Brittney Griner and Paul Whelan. His death occurred less than a week after a White House news conference that highlighted a temporary ceasefire in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia.

Darchiev was described by the Russian Foreign Ministry as an “exceptional professional” and “distinguished expert on the United States.” The ministry expressed condolences to his family and noted that his memory would remain with them. His death comes amid ongoing peace talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States, with recent discussions in Abu Dhabi and plans for further talks in Moscow.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News states that Darchiev died in Russia, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not specify the location of his death. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller mention that Darchiev was a “fierce critic of the West” and defended Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, while FOX News and Just The News do not attribute such characterizations to him. The New York Post notes that Darchiev was born to a Soviet diplomatic family in Hungary, a detail not included in other accounts. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller report that Darchiev was appointed as ambassador in March 2025, while FOX News and Just The News also state this, but The New York Post refers to his appointment as “last year,” which could imply 2025 or 2026 depending on the context.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Just The News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

New York building collapse kills at least two, officials say

A three-story building in Brooklyn collapsed into an open construction site on Wednesday afternoon, killing at least two people and injuring more than 17 others, according to multiple outlets. The incident occurred around 4 p.m. local time, triggering a massive search-and-rescue operation involving over 250 first responders. Aerial footage showed firefighters pulling a survivor, later identified as a pregnant woman, from the rubble. Officials have not yet confirmed the identities of those killed or injured. The building, constructed in 1930, was located near the corner of Bedford and Flatbush Avenues. Rescue efforts are expected to last several days due to the unstable conditions.

Witnesses described a loud explosion followed by screams as the building collapsed. One woman, Emmanuella Carilus, told the New York Times she lived behind the building and heard a "big boom." Another witness, Dashik, described the event as "I've never seen anything like this." The collapse exposed parts of the building's interior, including bedrooms and wardrobes, with debris including household items and clothes scattered across the site.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that officials say the death toll is rising and they do not know how many others are missing, while Just The News states that ABC 7 later corrected its initial report, indicating one person is still trapped and eight were injured. The Daily Wire mentions that a family of six lived in the building, known to Assemblywoman Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn, which is not mentioned in BBC or Al Jazeera. FOX News provides casualty figures of 19 patients, including two fatalities, four in critical condition, and 12 in stable condition, which is not included in the BBC or The Guardian accounts. Al Jazeera notes the building was in a predominantly Black and Afro-Caribbean community, a detail absent in other reports. The Guardian mentions seven children among the injured, a detail not included in BBC or FOX News.

Sources BBC · Just The News · The Daily Wire · Al Jazeera · The Guardian · FOX News

Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, health authorities say

An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a general surgeon, and wounded at least 28 more, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The strike occurred early Thursday, as reported by the Israeli military, which claimed it struck a Hamas commander and other militants without providing evidence. The hospital's surgical wing was hit, with parts of several floors severely damaged or destroyed. British surgeon Goher Rahbour, volunteering at the hospital, described the strike as occurring just after midnight, shaking the entire building and reducing the recovery area on the fourth floor to rubble. He noted that he had been operating alongside the deceased doctor, Rizk Abu Shaira, just hours before the strike.

The Israeli military accused Hamas of using the hospital as a command center for military and terrorist activities, stating that the commander had turned it into a headquarters. The hospital is one of the few functioning medical facilities in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been heavily damaged by years of conflict. Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital, including a strike in 2025 that killed five journalists, including an Associated Press contributor.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and CBS News both report that the strike killed six people and wounded at least 28 or a dozen more, respectively. BBC reports six killed and about 20 injured. NPR and CBS mention the Israeli military's claim of striking a Hamas commander and other militants, while BBC adds that the Israeli military said the commander had used the hospital as a "headquarters." CBS and BBC note that the Israeli military accused Hamas of using the hospital for military purposes, while NPR includes the military's statement about the commander turning the hospital into a headquarters. NPR and CBS mention the strike hit the surgical wing, while BBC specifies the missile hit the surgical wards and intensive care units. NPR and CBS report the strike occurred early Thursday, while BBC says it happened overnight. NPR and CBS include details about the hospital's condition and the impact on medical staff, while BBC adds that a paramedic described the missile penetrating the five-storey structure and hitting a room in the surgical department. NPR and CBS mention the hospital was hit in 2025, while BBC adds that it was hit by a double strike in August 2025, killing at least 20 people.

Sources NPR · CBS News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Admits to Affair with Woman Linked to Chinese Spy Allegations

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman linked to a Chinese spy scandal, according to multiple outlets. The affair, which Huang acknowledged in a letter to employees, has sparked an internal investigation by Nvidia's board. The woman, identified as Alice Huang, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that has been under scrutiny for potential violations of U.S. export controls. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about Nvidia and potentially influence its chip sales to China. Nvidia's stock price dropped by over 4% following the revelations. The controversy has also led to a shareholder lawsuit alleging that Nvidia and Huang misled investors about the affair and its national security implications.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that Huang's management style and his emphasis on resilience and character are central to Nvidia's success, while the other accounts focus on the affair and its national security implications. The Dispatch and Al Jazeera both mention the affair and the alleged spy connection, but Al Jazeera provides more detail about the investigation and the stock market reaction. The Guardian adds the legal aspect of the shareholder lawsuit and mentions Trump's comments about the FBI investigation. Axios provides specific details about Alice Huang's background and her company's ties to Nvidia, including financial transactions and corporate history. The BBC highlights the broader implications for the U.S.-China AI competition and the potential impact on national security.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Dispatch · Al Jazeera · The Guardian · Axios · BBC

Russell Brand Sentenced to Over 10 Years for Rape and Sexual Assault

Russell Brand, the British comedian and actor, was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison for rape and sexual assault following a trial in Southwark Crown Court. The conviction came after a four-week trial where a jury found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. The charges involved incidents dating back to 2004 and 2009. Brand was acquitted on two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. The judge, Joel Bennathan, described Brand as a "sexual predator" and noted his "staggering arrogance." The sentence includes nine years for rape and 18 months for sexual assaults, with Brand expected to serve at least seven years in prison and the remainder under restrictions. Six women made allegations against Brand, spanning from 1999 to 2009. Victim impact statements were read in court, detailing the trauma and long-term effects of the incidents.

Where the accounts differ

The Free Press reports that Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual assault but does not specify the number of charges or the exact sentence. CBS News and NPR provide detailed information on the charges, including the specific incidents and the length of the sentence. Slate mentions the Channel 4 documentary and the Sunday Times reporting that led to the trial, which are not referenced in the other accounts. The Daily Caller notes that Brand was acquitted on two rape charges and one attempted indecent assault charge, a detail not included in the Free Press or CBS News accounts. The BBC focuses on Jonathan Ross's reaction to the conviction and separate allegations against David Walliams, which are not part of the other accounts.

Sources The Free Press · CBS News · Slate · NPR · BBC · The Daily Caller

Kennedy family joins US lawsuits to block Trump’s ‘unlawful’ arch plan

The Kennedy family has filed a legal motion to halt the construction of President Donald Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, DC, arguing it would obscure the graves of their ancestors and the JFK Eternal Flame at Arlington National Cemetery. The motion was filed by veteran Washington lawyer Norm Eisen and the Democracy Defenders Fund, a centre-left legal advocacy group. The plaintiffs, including children and grandchildren of former Senators Robert F Kennedy and Edward M Kennedy, claim the arch would “fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites” and block the sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and the cemetery’s Arlington House. The lawsuit adds to existing legal challenges against the project, including from the governments of D.C., Virginia, and Arlington County, as well as Vietnam War veterans and a historian.

The project is part of Trump’s broader effort to reshape Washington, DC, including plans for a historic golf course renovation and threats to demolish the Kennedy Center. The National Capital Planning Commission, which is stacked with Trump allies, approved the arch’s design last week, but U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order, halting construction for 14 days. The White House has defended the project as a tribute to 250 years of American independence, though opponents argue it lacks proper legal authorization.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The New York Post both mention that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump appointee, did not join the litigation. CBS News and The Hill do not mention this detail. Al Jazeera and The New York Post also note that the Kennedy family members are represented by Norm Eisen and the Democracy Defenders Fund, while CBS News and The Hill do not specify the legal representatives. The Hill and CBS News refer to the National Capital Planning Commission’s vote, while Al Jazeera and The New York Post do not mention this.

Sources Al Jazeera · NPR · CBS News · Washington Examiner · The Hill · New York Post

California Voters Reject Billionaire Wealth Tax Proposition 40

California voters rejected Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires with a net worth exceeding $1 billion, by a margin of 52.8% to 47.2%. The measure, backed by healthcare unions and progressive politicians, aimed to fund healthcare, education, and food assistance. The Associated Press called the race late Monday night with 83% of votes counted. Opponents, including billionaires and some Democrats, argued the tax would harm the economy and drive away wealthy residents. Governor Gavin Newsom, a key opponent, warned it could undermine California’s economic competitiveness. The defeat of Prop 40 may slow nationwide momentum for wealth taxes, though supporters argue the measure’s existence represents progress.

Proposition 40 was sponsored by the healthcare union SEIU-UHW and supported by progressive figures like Rep. Ro Khanna and Sen. Bernie Sanders. Critics, including Newsom and tech billionaires, claimed the tax would disproportionately harm the state’s economy and tax base. The opposition campaign, led by billionaires like Sergey Brin, spent over $425 million, making it the most expensive ballot measure campaign in California history. Prop 42, which would ban future wealth taxes, remained ahead by 3.2 percentage points.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Guardian both report that Prop 40 was a one-time 5% tax on billionaires with a net worth over $1 billion, but only The Guardian specifies that the tax would have applied to individuals with a net worth of more than $1bn as of January 1, 2026. Mother Jones does not mention the exact date. The Guardian also states that Prop 40 was sponsored by SEIU-UHW, while Mother Jones refers to it as being sponsored by the healthcare workers union. The Daily Wire and Fox Business both mention that the tax would have been funded primarily for healthcare, but only The Daily Wire specifies that 90% of the money would have gone to healthcare. Mother Jones and The Guardian do not provide this detail. The Guardian and The Daily Wire both attribute the claim that the tax would have driven billionaires out of the state to critics, while Mother Jones attributes it to Rep. Khanna.

Sources Mother Jones · The Guardian · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Fox Business · The Daily Wire

Hardline Trump aide Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff

Stephen Miller, a key architect of Trump’s immigration policies, was appointed White House chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles. The move came after significant Republican losses in the midterm elections. Trump announced Miller’s promotion on Truth Social, despite earlier claims that Wiles would remain in her role. Miller, who has long supported Trump’s hardline immigration stance, is now in a more powerful position to influence the administration’s agenda. Trump acknowledged that his deportation policies were “too tough” in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes, though he still chose to elevate Miller.

Miller’s role has expanded beyond immigration, including advocating for anti-DEI mandates on campuses and leading efforts against suspected drug-smuggling boats. His appointment follows the departure of several top women in the administration, including Harmeet Dhillon and Katie Zacharia. Trump also mentioned offering Dana White, the UFC CEO, the press secretary role, though he later claimed it was a joke.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Nation both report that Trump claimed his deportation policies were “too tough” in an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes, while The Nation adds that Trump expressed a desire to strike a “grand deal” with Democrats to allow undocumented migrants to stay. The Daily Wire and Axios do not mention this interview or the proposed deal. The Guardian and The Nation attribute Trump’s comments to CBS’s 60 Minutes, while The Daily Wire and Axios do not specify the source of Trump’s remarks. The Mother Jones article includes details about Miller’s alleged mobster fandom and his wife’s shared interest, which are not mentioned in the other accounts. The Nation and The Guardian describe Miller as a “most zealous white nationalist,” while The Daily Wire and Axios do not make this characterization.

Sources The Guardian · The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · The Nation · NPR · Axios

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US reportedly evacuates aircraft from RAF Mildenhall over Iran threat

The US military evacuated aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England in response to a threat from Iran, according to multiple reports. The move involved refueling tankers and transport aircraft being relocated to bases in Germany, Spain, and Scotland, as well as Osprey transport planes sent to nearby RAF Lakenheath. This follows a similar redeployment of bombers from RAF Fairford in October after a security incident linked to Iran. The US has raised the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest defensive alert level. UK officials have stated that British bases remain secure, though the precise nature of the threat remains under discussion among US officials.

The incident comes amid heightened concerns about the security implications of the US-Israel war on Iran. Iranian officials have previously threatened to target UK bases used by the US military for strikes against Iran. The US has also faced criticism over the legality of its operations in the region, with former Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially opposing the use of UK bases for strikes against Iran.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and FOX News both report that 13 aircraft were evacuated from RAF Mildenhall, while the Christian Science Monitor and Al Jazeera do not specify a number. The Guardian and FOX News attribute the threat to Iran, while the Christian Science Monitor and Al Jazeera mention the broader context of the US-Israel war on Iran. The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that the US upgraded security at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to FPCON Charlie, while the Christian Science Monitor and FOX News provide more detail on the types of aircraft moved. The Guardian and FOX News mention the Wall Street Journal as a source, while the Christian Science Monitor and Al Jazeera do not. The Guardian and BBC do not mention the number of aircraft evacuated, while FOX News and the Christian Science Monitor do.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · Christian Science Monitor · FOX News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

France Blames Iran For Grocery Store Hack That Spoiled Food And Sparked Fires

French authorities accused Iranian hackers of targeting refrigeration systems at 700 grocery stores, causing food spoilage and fires. The Paris prosecutor’s office opened a judicial investigation, citing the attack as the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French territory. The hackers, linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), disabled refrigeration alarms and triggered endless defrost cycles, raising temperatures to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. The attack affected major chains like Intermarché and Coopérative U, with losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros. The French government warned of potential European sanctions against those responsible.

The FBI and other U.S. agencies issued a joint warning about similar risks to American grocery stores, urging operators to secure their systems. French officials traced the attack to IP addresses in Iran and noted the use of Farsi in the operation. The French government has summoned Iran’s ambassador to protest the attack, though Iran has not yet responded. The incident is part of a broader trend of attacks on refrigeration systems across Europe and the U.S., with some experts linking the attacks to Iranian hacking groups.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and CBS News both state that the attack caused roughly 20 fires, while Axios reports at least 15 fires. BBC mentions 20 fires but does not specify the exact number. NPR does not mention the number of fires at all. The Daily Wire and CBS News also note that the attack affected 700 stores, while BBC and Axios report 700 stores as well, but BBC adds that the attacks were followed by similar incidents in other European countries. NPR and Axios mention additional attacks on hydroelectric plants and blood banks, which are not detailed in the Daily Wire or CBS News. The Daily Wire and CBS News attribute the attack to the IRGC and Shahid Kaveh, while BBC and Axios also mention the same groups but note that Iran has not officially responded. NPR and Axios provide more context about the broader trend of attacks on refrigeration systems globally.

Sources The Daily Wire · BBC · NPR · CBS News · Axios

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Three dead after car strikes pedestrians in North Hollywood

A car struck pedestrians near a North Hollywood bus stop on Tuesday, resulting in three fatalities and three others in critical condition. The incident occurred around 5:55 p.m. local time. The Los Angeles Fire Department confirmed three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were transported to a nearby hospital. The driver, whose identity remains unknown, was hospitalized in critical condition. Authorities have launched an investigation into the circumstances of the crash.

The crash took place near a North Hollywood metro station and involved a white SUV that ran onto the sidewalk and collided with a mass-transit shelter structure. Aerial footage showed the partially crumpled vehicle. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass expressed her condolences for the victims, stating she was heartbroken for their families. The Los Angeles Police Department noted the driver was being evaluated for potential impairment and that the investigation is ongoing.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and CBS News both state the driver was hospitalized in critical condition, while FOX News and The Guardian attribute this information to the Los Angeles Police Department. The Guardian and CBS News mention the crash occurred near a North Hollywood metro station and a food stand, while FOX News and The New York Post refer to the incident as occurring near a North Hollywood Metro bus stop. The New York Post and CBS News report that the victims included street vendors, a detail not mentioned by The Guardian or FOX News. The Guardian and CBS News provide more specific details about the location, including Lankershim Boulevard, while FOX News and The New York Post do not specify the exact location beyond the Metro station.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · FOX News · New York Post · CBS News

Tennessee’s lethal drug supplier fears retaliation after Christa Pike’s botched execution: court docs

Christa Pike, a convicted murderer, survived a lethal injection execution attempt on Sept. 30, becoming the first death row inmate to do so. The execution, which involved two doses of pentobarbital administered with at least 10 needles, was botched and left Pike requiring round-the-clock medical care. Tennessee prison officials are now seeking to keep the identities of their lethal drug suppliers confidential, citing fears of retaliation. A Tennessee Department of Corrections employee filed court documents warning that suppliers may stop providing pentobarbital if their identities are exposed, which could halt executions in the state. The court documents were filed in response to a judge’s order to preserve evidence from the execution, including drug vials and needles.

Tennessee officials are urging a judge to keep the identities of their lethal injection drug suppliers secret, warning that exposure could lead to retaliation and the loss of pentobarbital suppliers. A state employee described the concerns of providers, who claim they are worried about threats, harassment, and boycotts due to their lawful role in supplying execution drugs. The employee warned that if the labels on drug vials are viewed by Pike’s legal team, the state may lose access to pentobarbital, potentially stopping executions. The judge has not yet ruled on the motion.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post states that Pike was set to become the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in over 200 years, while FOX News reports she was set to become the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in over two centuries. The New York Post mentions that Pike was moved to the infirmary at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center on Oct. 9 and requires round-the-clock care, while FOX News notes that Pike’s attorneys have sought to have her removed from the medical ward and placed back into a specialized, low-security unit. The New York Post does not mention an anesthesiologist advising Pike’s defense, which FOX News includes as part of its reporting.

Sources New York Post · FOX News
