House poised to impeach Pete Hegseth after GOP midterm defeat

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is forcing a House vote this week to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he violated the U.S. Constitution by engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization. The impeachment effort is seen as a political move to pressure President Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" led by a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and defended his record, claiming he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda. The House has not yet voted on the measure, but some GOP lawmakers, including Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), have indicated they may support the impeachment due to the GOP's midterm losses and growing frustration with the Iran war.

The impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of abusing his powers in relation to several Pentagon operations, including the Iran war, the seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters. While the measure is unlikely to pass with the current Republican majority, the midterm losses have emboldened some lawmakers to vote their consciences. The political calculus has shifted significantly since the election, with the GOP's defeat fueling anger within the conference and increasing the number of Republicans willing to back impeachment.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire states that the War Powers Resolution does not apply to the Secretary of Defense and that Massie's impeachment articles rely on a flawed legal theory, while Axios and The New York Post describe the impeachment as a political move targeting Hegseth's role in the Iran war. The Washington Examiner notes that Massie believes Hegseth is more likely to resign before Democratic-led hearings, a claim not made by other outlets. The BBC and The Hill both mention that Massie introduced the articles of impeachment in September, but The Daily Wire provides more detail on the legal basis of the case, including the specific clauses of the War Powers Resolution.

Sources Axios · BBC · The Hill · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · New York Post

Russell Brand Sentenced to 10 Years and 6 Months for Rape and Sexual Assault

British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault. The judge, Justice Joel Bennathan, called Brand a "sexual predator" and emphasized the severity of his crimes, noting that Brand used his fame to exploit women. The convictions stemmed from four incidents between 2004 and 2009, with the rape occurring at Brand's home in Hampstead, London. Six women testified against Brand in a four-week trial, detailing the impact of his actions on their lives. Brand's defense argued that the crimes were isolated and that he had changed significantly since the incidents. The judge added two years to the rape sentence due to aggravating factors, including the removal of a condom during the assault.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and CBS News both mention that Brand was seen holding white rosary beads during the proceedings, while the Guardian and NPR do not mention this detail. The Guardian and CBS News report that Brand was seen holding rosary beads, while the Daily Wire and NPR do not. The Daily Wire and CBS News describe Brand's wife, Laura, as being in court and interacting with him, while the Guardian and NPR do not specify this. The Guardian and CBS News mention that the judge added two years to the rape sentence for aggravating factors, while the Daily Wire and NPR do not specify the reason for the additional time. The Daily Wire and CBS News report that Brand was seen holding rosary beads during the proceedings, while the Guardian and NPR do not mention this detail.

Sources Slate · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · CBS News · BBC

Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections

U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume in Abu Dhabi this week, with European representatives expected to participate despite Russian objections. France's foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, confirmed France's involvement, though he did not specify who would represent the country. The talks, which will take place on Tuesday and Wednesday, are the first since February and follow a U.S. visit to Russia by envoy Steve Witkoff. The U.S. aims to address postwar security arrangements and de-escalation, with the Trump administration emphasizing the need for European involvement in any lasting peace deal. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concerns about the potential territorial concessions Ukraine may be required to make, warning of the risks involved.

The talks will include discussions on postwar security and humanitarian issues, with the U.S. seeking to involve European countries in shaping a new security framework. Russian delegation leader Vladimir Medinsky will again represent Moscow, alongside senior officials including Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin. The U.S. has also invited European allies to Abu Dhabi to hold separate discussions, aiming to integrate them into the broader security dialogue. Despite the U.S. optimism, analysts remain skeptical about the likelihood of significant progress, given the deepening divide over territorial control and security guarantees.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that the talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation, and that the U.S. think tank Institute for the Study of War suggested some Russian officials may have sought to slow down previous talks. The Guardian notes that the U.S. is seeking a "final end" to the war and that the talks are the first since the U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran. The New York Post mentions that Trump suggested Ukraine would end up with a "little bit different shape" and that Zelenskyy had not been given details of the agreement Trump referenced. The Daily Wire highlights Kushner's four priorities, including economic and humanitarian measures, while Axios emphasizes the U.S. focus on military working groups and the need for European involvement in security discussions.

Sources NPR · Axios · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · BBC

Trump admits deportation policy was ‘too tough’ despite promoting Stephen Miller

In a rare concession, President Donald Trump acknowledged during a CBS 60 Minutes interview that his deportation policy was “too tough” and admitted it may have hurt his political standing. He suggested he was open to an agreement with Democrats that would allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the U.S., while continuing to remove those convicted of serious crimes. Trump described the policy as both helping and hurting, noting that while people gave him high marks for closing the border and removing “bad” individuals, others were upset about deporting those with good jobs and paying taxes.

Trump also blamed the Iran war and rising gas prices for contributing to the Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections. He maintained that the military campaign against Iran was justified and said he would make the same decision again, though he acknowledged the conflict might not have been popular in the short term.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Hill both report that Trump acknowledged his deportation policy was “too tough” and that he was open to a deal with Democrats. However, The Guardian mentions that Trump elevated Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, while The Hill notes that Trump replaced Susie Wiles with Miller. The Hill also includes a quote from Sen. Thom Tillis criticizing Miller’s appointment, which is absent in The Guardian. The New York Post and BBC focus more on the Iran war, with the BBC reporting that Trump said renewed attacks on Iran were “highly unlikely,” while the New York Post states that Trump said the war was “effectively over” militarily. The Guardian and The Hill both mention the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, which the other accounts do not include.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · BBC · The Hill · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

House Republicans to elect a new leader as they look to rebuild from midterm defeat

House Republicans will meet behind closed doors to elect a new minority leader following their loss of majority in the midterm elections. The contest will be between current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan, a co-founder of the House Freedom Caucus. The election, conducted by secret ballot, is seen as a pivotal moment for the party as it seeks to regroup from losing over 40 seats. Scalise, a close Trump ally, has emphasized a "conservative and consensus-driven" approach, while Jordan has advocated for an "aggressive posture" in legislative battles. The outcome will shape the party's direction as it faces a new Congress under Democratic control.

The remaining legislative agenda for Republicans includes preventing a government shutdown, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, and confirming Trump's nominees. However, Democrats are expected to limit Republican influence, as they hold the majority in both chambers. Some Republicans, like Rep. Thomas Massie, are pushing for additional votes on impeachment and Epstein-related legislation, which could complicate the process. The party also faces internal divisions, with some members advocating for a more Trump-aligned leadership and others seeking a more moderate path.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the leadership race is between Scalise and Jordan, with Scalise emphasizing a "conservative and consensus-driven" approach and Jordan advocating for an "aggressive posture." The Washington Examiner omits details about the leadership race and focuses on the unfinished legislative business. Axios highlights the challenges of a lame-duck session, noting that Democrats may delay legislative fights until January. The Daily Wire emphasizes the urgency of passing the National Defense Authorization Act and mentions the possibility of a reconciliation package. The Daily Caller and FOX News focus on the broader implications of Democratic control, including potential impeachments and investigations, which are not covered in the other accounts.

Sources NPR · Washington Examiner · Axios · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Judge Sets Charlie Kirk Trial Date — And It’s A Long Way Off

Judge Tony Graf Jr. has set the trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk, for June 21, 2028. The trial will begin in Provo, Utah, with jury selection starting on June 21. Prosecutors had requested a January 2028 start date to avoid holidays, while defense attorneys sought a late 2029 start. The trial is expected to last 17 weeks. Robinson, 23, is accused of fatally shooting Kirk on September 10, 2025, at Utah Valley University. He faces seven charges, including aggravated murder, which could result in the death penalty if convicted. Kirk’s wife, Erika Kirk, has argued for a faster trial, citing her right to a speedy trial under Utah law.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and FOX News both state that the trial is set for June 2028, while The Guardian and BBC report the trial will start in early July 2028 and June 2028 respectively. ABC News does not specify a month for the June 2028 trial. The Guardian and BBC mention that jury selection would begin on June 21, 2028, while The Daily Wire and FOX News do not specify the exact start date. The Guardian and BBC report that prosecutors expect the trial to last 17 weeks, while The Daily Wire and FOX News mention a 17-week trial and a potential six to seven-month duration. The Guardian and BBC include details about a video statement from Robinson’s roommate, Lance Twiggs, which The Daily Wire and FOX News do not mention. The Daily Wire and FOX News include statements from Donald Trump, which are absent in The Guardian and BBC. The Guardian and BBC mention that prosecutors presented DNA evidence and confessions, while The Daily Wire and FOX News do not specify the nature of the evidence.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · ABC News · BBC · FOX News

Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas. The decision came after the federal government filed an emergency request to lift a lower court's temporary halt on construction. The court ruled that the federal judge who issued the injunction did not have the authority to block the project, allowing the government to proceed with its plans. The Trump administration argued that the construction is necessary to secure the border and prevent illegal crossings, citing the need to address gaps in "border defenses."

The construction plans include physical walls, access roads, and surveillance systems in the Big Bend region, which spans over 500 miles and covers more than a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border. The project has faced bipartisan opposition, with residents and environmental groups arguing that the construction threatens the natural landscape, wildlife, and local economies. The Center for Biological Diversity and other groups have challenged the plans, claiming they violate environmental protections and harm public lands.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both mention that the Trump administration's plans for the Big Bend region have provoked bipartisan backlash, while ABC News and FOX News also note this opposition. However, ABC News specifically includes a quote from Charlie Angell, a landowner in Redford, Texas, who describes the impact of the construction on his business. The Guardian and NPR mention that the construction plans initially included a physical wall but were changed to include only vehicle barriers, roads, and surveillance technology due to public outcry. FOX News and The Daily Caller do not mention this change. The Guardian and NPR also note that the construction plans include a 17-mile barrier in Big Bend National Park, while FOX News states that the park will not feature the 30-foot steel fencing planned in other areas. The Daily Caller mentions that Texas recently elected a Democratic governor, which is not included in the other accounts.

Sources NPR · ABC News · FOX News · The Guardian · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Trump Just Offered the Press Secretary Gig to UFC’s Dana White

President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he had offered the position of White House press secretary to Dana White, CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). In a post on Truth Social, Trump described White as "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" and requested that he bring along several UFC fighters as assistants. The fighters named included Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris, though the latter’s name was misspelled. Trump claimed the fighters would "defend us against the Lunatic Left." White, who has no governmental experience, has been a long-time friend and business associate of Trump, having owned UFC since 2001. The offer comes as Trump’s administration is undergoing significant changes following the midterm elections, with White House press secretary positions remaining vacant after the brief tenure of Katie Zacharia.

White, who was in London for a boxing event, stated he planned to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House. He did not clarify whether he was seriously considering the position, though he expressed ambitions to expand his Zuffa Boxing organization. The White House and UFC did not immediately respond to inquiries about the offer.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Hill both report that Trump misspelled Kayla Harrison’s name as "Kayla Harris." Al Jazeera and The Hill note that Trump initially posted the offer on Truth Social, while Washington Examiner reports that Trump also posted an animated AI-generated video of UFC fighters attacking the press corps. FOX News, however, does not mention the press secretary offer at all, instead reporting on a separate claim by Trump about ordering a DOJ investigation into Democrats.

Sources Mother Jones · NPR · Al Jazeera · The Hill · Washington Examiner · FOX News

Jensen Huang spy scandal rocks AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an independent investigation by the company. Huang, who has led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, apologized to his family and employees, acknowledging his infidelity. The company stated it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. U.S. officials believe the woman, identified as Alice Huang, was recruited by Beijing's intelligence agency to gather information and potentially influence Nvidia's business dealings with China. The scandal has led to questions about the White House's awareness of the situation and its impact on U.S.-China relations.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Trump was briefed in 2025 and that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified intelligence memo in spring 2025. Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not specify the exact timing of the briefing but note that Trump was aware of the intelligence. Fox Business and The Guardian mention that Trump invited Huang to join his delegation to China in May, while Axios and Al Jazeera state that Huang was invited to the state dinner with Xi Jinping in September. The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that Huang described his interactions with Alice Huang as "completely normal and not unusual," while Axios and Fox Business report that Huang admitted to a romantic relationship with her.

Sources Axios · Al Jazeera · The Guardian · Fox Business · BBC · Newsweek

Gen Z voters helped Democrats win midterms with strong margins

Gen Z voters, those under 30, played a key role in Democrats' success in the 2026 midterms, according to exit polling. They carried the youngest generation by nearly 50 points, a sharp contrast to 2024 when the party lost ground with young voters. The shift is attributed to strong opposition to Trump and economic frustrations. Economic issues were the top concern for 18-29 year olds, with 43% citing it as their main issue. Over 80% of young voters said Trump's policies worsened economic conditions. Democrats also made gains with some young voters who had previously supported Trump, including white men and Latino men.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote and that Democrats flipped seats in House and Senate races, with Texas Senator James Talarico winning by 60 points among Gen Z voters. Mother Jones and The Hill focus on Trump's reaction to the losses, with The Hill noting Trump's admission that his immigration policies might have been "too tough." CBS News and The Dispatch provide details on Trump's interview with Ross Douthat, where he blamed the war in Iran and gas prices for the losses. BBC highlights the internal Republican party conflict and the potential for a split between Trump loyalists and more moderate Republicans. The Dispatch also notes the shift in voter priorities, with the economy, corruption, and governance being key concerns.

Sources NPR · Mother Jones · CBS News · The Hill · BBC · The Dispatch

Trump staffing changes post-midterms signal he's battle ready

President Donald Trump announced the replacement of his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller, a hard-liner known for his role in shaping Trump's controversial policies. The move comes after a significant loss for Republicans in the midterms. Trump has expressed openness to working with Democrats, though his appointment of Miller suggests a different approach. Miller, who has been a key advisor to Trump, is described by some as a staunch ideologue and is seen as a loyal supporter of the president's agenda.

The new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is known for his role in implementing Trump's immigration policies, including mass deportation raids. His appointment has drawn criticism from Democrats, who argue that his policies have led to significant backlash and have been associated with incidents involving the deaths of American citizens. Miller's appointment is seen as a signal of continued hardline policies and a potential escalation in the political conflict with the newly elected Democratic majority.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Trump described the Democratic Party as a "domestic extremist organization," while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller attribute this characterization to Stephen Miller. The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire mention that Hakeem Jeffries claims Miller is responsible for the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, a claim not made by NPR or Axios. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller include specific details about the incidents involving Pretti and Good, which are not present in the other accounts. Axios does not mention Jeffries's comments about Miller's responsibility for the deaths, while The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire do.

Sources NPR · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Axios

Democrats plan legislative agenda, avoid impeachment as Congress shifts power

Following the midterm elections, Democrats are preparing to take control of both the House and Senate in January. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton urged the party to focus on enacting their legislative agenda. Meanwhile, Democratic leaders have outlined priorities such as re-implementing Affordable Care Act provisions, undoing Medicaid cuts, and addressing Trump's tariffs. The party also plans to push for legislation that could serve as a platform for future presidential candidates. However, impeachment of Trump is not on the table, despite ongoing investigations into his actions.

The lame-duck session of Congress faces a looming government shutdown deadline on December 11, with both parties needing to reach an agreement on funding. Republicans are expected to push for a short-term extension, while Democrats may use Trump's actions in Iran as leverage. The Senate and House will also tackle the farm bill, transportation infrastructure, and a bipartisan tax package before the year ends.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Democrats are focusing on legislative action to prepare for the 2028 presidential election, including passing bills on price gouging, Super PACs, and stock trading by lawmakers. This is not mentioned in the Washington Examiner, which only notes Clinton's call for legislative action. The Guardian also states that the Democratic party brand remains deeply unpopular, a claim not present in the Washington Examiner. The New York Post and FOX News differ in their coverage of the shutdown deadline, with the New York Post noting that Democrats may use Trump's Iran actions as leverage, while FOX News reports that some Republicans expect a short-term funding extension through February or March.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · Just The News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · FOX News

CENTCOM Launches Lifestyle Podcast Amid Ongoing Iran Conflict

The United States Central Command (CENTCOM) launched a lifestyle podcast titled "Inside CENTCOM" on Thursday, featuring Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of CENTCOM. The podcast, which has been compared to a comedic show with a military twist, includes topics such as patience, physical fitness, and personal anecdotes. Cooper discussed his love for French fries and emphasized the importance of mental and spiritual fitness during military operations. The podcast's first episode lasted 11 minutes and did not address the ongoing conflict with Iran. Meanwhile, the U.S. military has been conducting "minor strikes" against Iran's Qeshm Island, with President Trump describing the attacks as a necessary measure to protect Israel. The war in Iran has been widely criticized as a costly and unpopular endeavor, with over 3,400 civilians killed and the U.S. military spending at least $47 billion.

The war in Iran has become a focal point for political blame, with Democrats attributing the conflict's negative consequences to the Trump administration. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a top Democrat, has publicly supported impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, calling him a "hard yes" for impeachment. Jeffries accused Hegseth of abusing his power and engineering a costly war of choice. Meanwhile, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie plans to reintroduce an impeachment resolution against Hegseth, citing violations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Trump has defended Hegseth, claiming he has done a "fantastic job" and intends to keep him in his position.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that the podcast "fields zero questions about the war," while New York Post and The Guardian do not mention this detail. The Guardian and ABC News describe the impeachment effort as a political move, while Mother Jones and Axios note that the impeachment is part of a broader political blame game. The New York Post and The Guardian mention the potential for a diplomatic breakthrough, which is not included in Mother Jones or Axios. The Guardian and ABC News attribute the war's costs and consequences to Hegseth, while Mother Jones and Axios attribute them to the Trump administration.

Sources Mother Jones · New York Post · BBC · Axios · The Guardian · ABC News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US launches task force to disrupt Iran’s land-based supply routes

The United States military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday the establishment of a new task force, Task Force Iron Gate, aimed at blocking Iran’s land-based supply routes. The task force will work with US government agencies to prevent the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s borders and the Caspian Sea. CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper stated that the task force will reinforce the existing naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz. A commercial cargo vessel, the M/V Huda, was disabled in the Gulf of Oman as part of the ongoing blockade. Iran’s official news agency IRNA reported explosions on Qeshm Island and in other cities near the Strait of Hormuz, while the IRGC Navy reported two oil tankers struck mines near the strait.

Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera that the task force’s role will be to identify where weapons systems are coming in and how they could be cut off. He suggested that if President Trump orders an escalation, it would likely involve attacks on economic and infrastructure targets. Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi confirmed that Iran had lifted its previous 2,000-kilometer ballistic missile-range restriction, according to The Associated Press.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Iran’s IRGC Navy said two oil tankers struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz, while FOX News attributes the mine strikes to the IRGC Navy but does not mention the tankers. Al Jazeera also notes that Trump downplayed strikes on Qeshm Island as “minor,” while FOX News does not mention this. Washington Examiner does not report on the mine strikes or Trump’s comments. FOX News reports that Iran lifted its ballistic missile-range limit and that Mohebbi warned of new weapons that would “astonish the entire world,” which is not mentioned in Al Jazeera or Washington Examiner. Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner do not mention the missile-range limit or Mohebbi’s comments about new weapons.

Sources Al Jazeera · FOX News · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left covered this story.

Dave Chappelle Says He ‘Feels Better’ Since Charlie Kirk’s Murder

Comedian Dave Chappelle made comments during a stand-up set in New York City on Friday that he “feels better” since conservative activist Charlie Kirk was fatally shot in September 2025. Chappelle told the audience, “Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered … and I shouldn’t say this publicly but, I feel better.” He also said, “I know I shouldn’t say that, but it’s just a feeling.” Chappelle has reportedly made similar remarks at other events during his “Karmageddon” tour. Charlie Kirk was shot at Utah Valley University, where he was speaking at an outdoor event.

Dave Chappelle’s comments came after leftist podcasters Jennifer Welch and Angie “Pumps” Sullivan discussed “digging up” Charlie Kirk’s body on their podcast. The hosts laughed at the idea of “digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again,” which led to sponsors dropping their support. The pair apologized, stating they regretted laughing at the joke and pledged to support gun safety reform.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and New York Post both report that Chappelle said he “feels better” since Kirk’s murder, while Newsweek provides more context about the broader controversies in Chappelle’s career, including his 2005 departure from his comedy show, 2017 transgender jokes, 2019 LGBTQ-related material, and 2021 remarks about transgender people. The Daily Wire and New York Post attribute Chappelle’s comments to a stand-up set in New York City, while Newsweek specifies the event was at Madison Square Garden. The Daily Wire and New York Post also mention that Chappelle previously spoke about Kirk in his Netflix special “The Unstoppable,” while Newsweek does not include this detail. The Daily Wire and New York Post attribute the claim that Chappelle “shouldn’t say this publicly” to Chappelle himself, while Newsweek does not attribute the quote.

Sources The Daily Wire · Newsweek · New York Post · ABC News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

In the 2026 midterm elections, Gen Z men shifted significantly from supporting Republicans to Democrats, according to multiple accounts. The New York Times reported that 70 percent of voters aged 18-29 cast their ballots for Democrats, a 33-point shift from 2024. The Guardian noted that Gen Z men, who had been a key part of Trump’s 2024 coalition, moved decisively toward Democrats, with 59 percent of white men aged 18-29 voting Democratic. The Hill highlighted that Gen Z men had been an important constituency for Trump in 2024, but in 2026, Democrats pulled them across the aisle. The Washington Examiner noted that Democrats took 50 percent of Gen Z men to the GOP’s 48 percent, marking a significant shift.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and The Washington Examiner both report that Gen Z men shifted from Republicans to Democrats, but they differ in the exact percentages. Sources The Hill · Mother Jones · The Daily Wire · Newsweek · The Guardian · Washington Examiner

Trump asks UFC chief Dana White to be White House press secretary

White stated he plans to meet with Trump at the White House on Monday to discuss the offer. Trump described White as “a violent Fighter and Warrior” and requested that he bring six UFC fighters as assistants to “defend us against the Lunatic Left.” The press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia’s brief tenure ended last month.

White, who has no governmental experience, has been a longtime ally of Trump and has attended several UFC events with him. The White House press office already includes a former UFC spokesperson, Steven Cheung, who worked for White’s organization from 2013 to 2016. White did not confirm whether he would accept the position, stating he has “a lot of jobs already.”

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both note that White has no fighting record or governmental record, while Mother Jones and Washington Examiner do not mention this detail. Sources Al Jazeera · Mother Jones · NPR · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Guardian

US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu

The US midterm elections, which saw Democrats gain control of Congress, are seen as a potential catalyst for Israeli opposition parties to unite and challenge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Guardian reports that the shift in US politics could pressure Netanyahu, who has aligned with Donald Trump’s Republicans, to step down. The opposition, led by Yair Lapid, has criticized Netanyahu’s close ties with the US Republicans, arguing that this has made Israel’s foreign policy less stable. Meanwhile, the election results have also highlighted the growing influence of Arab-led parties in Israeli politics, which won an unprecedented 19 seats. These parties, which have historically been marginalized, are now seen as key players in forming a new government. The Guardian also notes that incoming Democratic lawmakers, including Jewish Congressman Brad Lander, have criticized Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank, particularly the detention of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, which they argue violates international law.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and FOX News differ on the role of Arab-led parties in forming a government. The Guardian states that Arab-led parties won 19 seats and are now seen as potential kingmakers, while FOX News mentions that these parties recommended Eisenkot to the president but their support presents a dilemma for some of his prospective coalition partners. The Guardian also includes details about the detention of Abed Abu Shehada and the response from Congressman Brad Lander, which FOX News omits. The BBC and CBS News both mention that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot's bloc secured a majority, but the BBC adds that the president has broad discretion in choosing the next leader, while CBS News notes that Herzog's decision is a setback for Netanyahu.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · NPR · Al Jazeera · CBS News · FOX News

6 dead, 15 injured in market square shooting in Poland: Police

A gunman opened fire in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday, killing at least six people and injuring 15 others, according to Polish authorities. The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, was shot and wounded by police during a confrontation before being taken into custody. Three bodies were found at his home, identified as his parents and sister, according to Prime Minister Donald Tusk. The attack occurred near Slawkowska Street, with the suspect driving a car and firing at random people. Police confirmed the suspect was not a soldier but wore military-style clothing and used an AR-15-style rifle. The incident led to citywide mourning, with flags lowered and events canceled.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and The Guardian both report that the suspect was wearing military-style camouflage clothing, while Newsweek and BBC describe him as wearing military-style fatigues. ABC News and CBS News mention that the suspect was armed with an AR-15-style rifle, while The Guardian and BBC refer to a military-type long gun. Washington Examiner reports 5 dead and 12 injured, while ABC News, CBS News, and The Guardian report 6 dead and 15 injured. Newsweek and BBC state that the suspect was wearing a bulletproof vest, which is not mentioned in ABC News or CBS News. The Guardian and BBC mention that the suspect fired at a tram, which is not reported by ABC News or CBS News.

Sources ABC News · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · BBC · CBS News · The Guardian

Houston mayor curbs cooperation of US city’s police with ICE

Houston Mayor John Whitmire issued an executive order limiting the city’s police force cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Under the new policy, police will only contact ICE when a person is arrested for a jailable offense. The order was announced days after Democrats won all Texas statewide offices. The move aims to reduce fear and anxiety among residents, particularly immigrants.

The policy reverses a previous directive Whitmire had implemented in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott. Abbott had threatened to withhold $110 million in state public safety grants if Houston did not comply with state law requiring cooperation with ICE. Whitmire stated he consulted Texas’s newly elected state leaders before acting, and that the change was intended to create a model for other cities.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both report that Houston police contacted ICE at least 107 times in the first eight months of 2025, compared to nine times in 2024. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention this specific statistic. The Guardian also notes that an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July, while FOX News and The Daily Wire refer to this incident but do not specify the month. The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire mention the October incident involving ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales, which The Guardian does not include.

Sources Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · The Daily Wire · FOX News · The Daily Caller

Secret Service arrests Venezuelan man near White House with multiple firearms after alleged threat to kill Trump

A Venezuelan national was arrested near the White House after being found in a stolen vehicle with multiple firearms, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Secret Service officers spotted the vehicle parked on Constitution Avenue near the White House complex shortly before midnight on Thursday. When approached, the suspect allegedly told officers he had heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C., and kill President Trump. A search of the vehicle revealed a MAC-10 machine pistol, a Glock 43x pistol, an AR-15 rifle, and dozens of rounds of ammunition. The suspect, Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, is undocumented and entered the U.S. through Texas in 2024.

The suspect was charged with multiple firearms and vehicle-related offenses, including unauthorized use of a vehicle, receiving stolen property, and carrying a pistol and rifle without a license. He made an initial appearance in D.C. Superior Court and remains held without bond. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed the arrest and stated the suspect was in custody with the U.S. Marshals Service.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News states the suspect is named Ronny Guanipa-Chrinos, while Washington Examiner, FOX News, The Daily Wire, The Guardian, and CBS News refer to him as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos. ABC News mentions the suspect allegedly told investigators through Google Translate, "I have the gun because they tried to kill me with it, and I had to take it away from them; it's in the brown bag," which is omitted by other outlets. FOX News and The Daily Wire include details about the suspect being released under the Biden administration and having a detainer lodged by ICE, which are not mentioned in ABC News. The Guardian does not mention the specific firearms found, while CBS News includes a photo of the seized items.

Sources ABC News · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News

US carries out strikes on Iranian air defenses as talks continue

The US military conducted strikes on Iranian air defenses on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to multiple outlets. President Trump described the strikes as “minor” and claimed they took about 15 minutes to execute. The strikes occurred after a series of attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, with at least 11 ships targeted over the past week, though the number of ships sunk varies between reports. The US is also applying economic pressure on Iran through a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which has reportedly bottled up $25 billion in Iranian crude oil. Talks between the US and Iran to end the war continue, with Qatar acting as a mediator. The US has offered a reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program, and both sides have engaged in diplomatic discussions.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Guardian both report that the US conducted strikes on Qeshm Island, but the New York Post mentions that the strikes were the first since the midterms, while The Guardian does not specify the timing of the strikes relative to the election. The Guardian reports that at least 11 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, while the New York Post cites the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations for the same figure. The Guardian also notes that the strikes are the first since the midterms, a detail not included in the New York Post. The Guardian mentions the US offering a $20 million reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program, which is not mentioned in the New York Post. The Guardian also reports that the strikes are the first since the midterms, a detail not included in the New York Post.

Sources New York Post · Christian Science Monitor · The Federalist · The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Former US senator and West Virginia governor Jay Rockefeller dies at 89

Jay Rockefeller, a former U.S. senator and governor of West Virginia, died at the age of 89. He was born into the prominent Rockefeller family and served in the Senate for nearly 30 years. Rockefeller was known for his advocacy of expanded healthcare and social policies, and for his criticism of the Iraq War. He was also a key supporter of President Bill Clinton’s failed health care initiative and President Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act. His death was reported by multiple outlets, with his family confirming the news but not disclosing the cause.

Rockefeller was elected to the Senate in 1984 after serving as West Virginia’s secretary of state and two terms as governor. He chaired several Senate committees, including the Intelligence Committee, and led an investigation into the Bush administration’s pre-war intelligence assessments. He initially supported the Iraq War but later expressed regret, calling the decision based on "false premises." He retired from the Senate in 2015 and was remembered by colleagues and family members for his dedication to public service and his state.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Rockefeller was described by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito as a "true gentleman" and that Sen. Joe Manchin called him a "mentor." The Daily Wire and New York Post provide more detailed accounts of Rockefeller’s political career, including his support for Clinton’s health care plan and his regret over the Iraq War vote. Straight Arrow News mentions his early work with Volunteers in Service to America and his role in establishing the Children’s Health Insurance Program. The Washington Examiner and CBS News focus more on his personal background and family connections, including his great-grandfather John D. Rockefeller and his uncle Nelson Rockefeller. The Daily Wire and CBS News both mention his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, and their four children, while FOX News and New York Post do not specify the number of children.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · New York Post · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: New Jersey town's $26M theft undermines public trust and threatens essential services as mayor delayed disclosure until after the election.

New Jersey town reveals $26M theft days after election, sparking backlash

A New Jersey township, Cranbury, disclosed a fraudulent wire transfer of approximately $26 million on November 6, more than five weeks after the theft occurred. The funds were intended for purchasing property to meet the township's affordable housing obligations. Mayor Lisa Knierim, a Democrat, announced the theft, stating it was a "sophisticated financial theft" that took place on September 28. The township is working with a task force involving local, county, state, and federal law enforcement to recover the funds. So far, nearly $17.3 million in assets have been frozen, leaving about $8.7 million unaccounted for. The mayor acknowledged residents' concerns about the delayed disclosure and noted that the Township Committee plans to introduce new positions to strengthen financial oversight.

The disclosure came three days after the midterm elections, in which Democrat Thomas Szczur Jr. defeated Republican Carol Haring, securing Democratic control of all five seats on the Cranbury Township Committee. Residents expressed frustration over the timing of the announcement, with some demanding greater transparency and questioning the delay in disclosure.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News states that the mayor's announcement came three days after Election Day and more than five weeks after the theft, while the New York Post confirms the same timeline. Both outlets report that the township is working with a task force to recover the funds and that $17.3 million has been frozen. FOX News mentions that the mayor's statement was published on the township's Facebook page, while the New York Post attributes the mayor's statement to NJ.com. The New York Post includes additional resident comments and jokes, which FOX News does not mention. FOX News notes that the mayor's office was reached for additional comment, while the New York Post does not mention this.

Sources FOX News · New York Post

Trump Names Stephen Miller as New White House Chief of Staff

President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Stephen Miller, his deputy chief of staff, will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting November 9, 2026. The move comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Miller, known for his hardline immigration policies, is expected to continue Trump's agenda, including efforts to strengthen border security and end birthright citizenship. Wiles, who had been a key figure in the administration, resigned following the election results.

Trump described Miller as a "great fighter" and "very loyal," emphasizing his role in the administration's successes. The president also mentioned that Miller's appointment signals a continuation of his policies, particularly on immigration, which has been a central focus of his administration. The decision follows a period of significant political shifts, with Democrats gaining control of Congress and Trump facing criticism for his approach to immigration and other issues.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Daily Wire both state that Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," while Newsweek and Washington Examiner refer to him as "one of the most influential and uncompromising figures in his administration." The Daily Wire and Mother Jones mention that Wiles resigned after the midterm losses, while Newsweek and Washington Examiner attribute her resignation to the election results. The Daily Wire and The Washington Examiner note that Miller is described as a "wartime consigliere" by a source close to the White House, a characterization not included in other accounts. The Daily Wire and The Washington Examiner also mention that Trump's move to promote Miller gained support from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a detail absent in other reports.

Sources Mother Jones · Newsweek · BBC · Washington Examiner · Just The News · The Daily Wire

US judge halts construction of Trump’s triumphal arch in Washington, DC

A federal judge ordered a 14-day pause on the construction of President Donald Trump’s 250-foot “triumphal arch” in Washington, DC, following a court ruling. The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) approved the project with an 8-4 vote, despite opposition from dozens of witnesses. The judge’s decision follows multiple lawsuits challenging the construction, including one from Vietnam war veterans who argued the arch would block the view between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Trump has proposed building the arch near Arlington National Cemetery, where war veterans are buried, raising concerns about its impact on the cemetery’s visibility.

The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers, and veterans, who argue it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Trump has also claimed the arch would be converted into a military complex capable of deploying drones and storing ammunition. The White House has stated the arch would commemorate 250 years of US independence, comparing it to the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. The judge’s order temporarily blocks construction, excavation, and other preparatory activities, requiring the administration to certify compliance by November 9.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Hill both report that the judge cited concerns about traffic, disaster preparedness, and environmental harm as reasons for the pause. Mother Jones and Axios note that the judge also referenced the need for congressional authorization and compliance with federal requirements. FOX News and Axios mention that Trump has previously claimed the arch would include military capabilities, such as snipers and drone deployment, which are not explicitly mentioned in Al Jazeera or The Hill. The Hill and Axios state that the judge ordered the government to file a status report by November 9, while Al Jazeera and The Hill do not mention this detail. Mother Jones and Axios also highlight that the NCPC vote was packed with over 100 public comments, mostly against the project, which is not explicitly stated in Al Jazeera or The Hill.

Sources Al Jazeera · FOX News · Washington Examiner · Mother Jones · Axios · The Hill

Gavin Newsom Has Commuted the Largest Death Row in the Western Hemisphere

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state to life without the possibility of parole. Newsom, who is term-limited and will leave office in January, described the action as incompatible with California’s values and a failure of the legal system. The decision comes after California has not executed anyone since 2006, and Newsom had previously instituted a formal moratorium on executions in 2019. The move is seen as symbolic, as the state has not carried out an execution in over two decades. Newsom’s successor, Xavier Becerra, has committed to extending the execution moratorium once in office.

Newsom’s commutations must be individually approved by California’s courts, and the state Supreme Court will review cases where the individual was convicted of multiple felonies. The United States has executed 33 people in 2026 so far, though most executions are carried out at the state level. Newsom’s decision has been praised by civil rights advocates and some victims’ families, who argue that the death penalty is costly and unreliable. However, prosecutors and some victims’ relatives have criticized the move, arguing it undermines justice for victims and fails to address the severity of the crimes committed.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Guardian both state that Newsom’s commutations will convert all death sentences to life without parole, while FOX News and The New York Post highlight specific cases, such as Isauro Aguirre, who murdered an 8-year-old boy, and Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and murdered Polly Klaas. The Guardian and Mother Jones mention that 220 inmates waited 15 years or more for legal representation, a detail not included in other accounts. The Hill notes that 70% of the commutations will require review by the California Supreme Court, a point not mentioned in other outlets. The New York Post and FOX News emphasize the political nature of the decision, while Mother Jones and The Guardian focus on the moral and legal arguments.

Sources Mother Jones · BBC · The Guardian · FOX News · New York Post · The Hill

Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault

Russell Brand, 51, was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury at Southwark Crown Court in London. The verdict followed a four-week trial involving six women who alleged incidents spanning from 1999 to 2009. Brand was acquitted of two rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, remanded Brand in custody pending sentencing, which is scheduled for Monday. Brand, who had pleaded not guilty to the charges, showed little emotion during the verdict and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken into custody. The Metropolitan Police stated that Brand remains under investigation for two further rape allegations.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Al Jazeera both report that Brand was found guilty of anally raping a young fan at his London townhouse in 2009, while the Guardian adds that the victim begged him to stop but he continued. CBS News and Newsweek describe the same incident but do not mention the victim begging him to stop. The Guardian and Newsweek also note that Brand was cleared of orally raping the woman in a toilet after the 2004 incident, while CBS News and Al Jazeera do not specify this detail. The Guardian and Newsweek mention that the victim described feeling like she couldn't speak or breathe due to the pain, a detail not included in the other accounts. The Guardian and Al Jazeera state that Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman at a London bar in 2004, while CBS News and Newsweek describe the same incident but do not specify the location as a bar. The Guardian and Newsweek also mention that Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman while working on a promotional project, while CBS News and Al Jazeera do not specify this detail.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · CBS News · Al Jazeera · ABC News · Newsweek

DOJ's Harmeet Dhillon resigns

Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general for civil rights at the Justice Department, has resigned from her role, Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday. Dhillon spearheaded the DOJ's efforts to monitor midterm elections in all 50 states for the first time in U.S. history, sending approximately 1,000 monitors to ensure "election integrity." She was appointed by President Trump in December 2024 and confirmed by the Senate in April 2025. The DOJ referred Axios' request for comment to Blanche's post.

Two top Justice Department officials resigned Friday, including the prosecutor whose South Florida office oversaw President Trump’s so-called grand conspiracy probe. Jason Reding Quinones, the South Florida-based U.S. attorney tasked with leading a sweeping and controversial conspiracy probe targeting President Donald Trump's foes, has resigned from the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Friday. The dual resignations came in quick succession, with Blanche sharing just an hour and a half later that John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, was also departing.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and The Guardian both report Dhillon's resignation and her role in the DOJ's election monitoring, but only The Guardian details the extent of her transformation of the civil rights division, including dropping cases against racial minorities and the exodus of career lawyers. The Guardian also includes quotes from Kristen Clarke and Stacey Young criticizing Dhillon's leadership. ABC News and The Hill mention Dhillon's resignation but do not provide the same level of detail about her impact on the civil rights division. Straight Arrow News and The Hill both describe Dhillon's background and prior experience, but only The Hill notes her role in the Trump administration's efforts to challenge transgender policies. The Dispatch does not cover the event at all.

Sources Axios · ABC News · Straight Arrow News · The Hill · The Dispatch · The Guardian

Colom and Hyde-Smith's razor-thin Senate race spotlights Mississippi's voter rolls

The Mississippi Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith remains too close to call, with Colom holding a narrow lead of over 2,000 votes as of Friday. The race has drawn attention due to the state's use of provisional ballots and a controversial voter-roll cleanup. Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson announced that 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots remain to be counted, along with an unknown number of provisional ballots. These ballots are required for voters who lacked proper identification or had their addresses changed. The state's system allows for these ballots to be counted if they were postmarked by Election Day and received by November 10. The race has also raised concerns about the reliability of third-party data used to verify voter addresses, particularly after a $50,000 deal with Experian in March. Election officials in Oktibbeha County confirmed that some records were inaccurate, with one voter being incorrectly told he lived in a different county. The race has led to legal disputes over how provisional ballots should be handled, with both campaigns preparing for potential legal challenges.

Where the accounts differ

AXIOS reports that the number of inactive voters increased from 166,000 in 2024 to over 230,000 ahead of the midterms, while FOX News does not mention the number of inactive voters. BBC states that Colom leads by 2,500 votes, while AXIOS and THE FEDERALIST report Colom leading by over 2,000 votes. THE DAILY WIRE and AXIOS both mention that 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots remain to be counted, but THE FEDERALIST adds that 17,000 affidavit ballots are also pending. THE FEDERALIST and STRAIGHT ARROW NEWS both mention that provisional ballots are being quarantined, but STRAIGHT ARROW NEWS does not specify the number of such ballots. STRAIGHT ARROW NEWS and THE DAILY WIRE both mention that the final results could be delayed until November 13, but STRAIGHT ARROW NEWS also notes that Wall Street has reacted to the election results, a detail not present in other accounts.

Sources Axios · FOX News · BBC · Straight Arrow News · The Daily Wire · The Federalist

Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights in a week

Bomb threats disrupted at least 20 European flights in a week, with several diverted to military bases or subjected to security checks. Authorities confirmed no explosives were found on any of the planes, and the incidents were deemed hoaxes. The threats have raised concerns about potential coordination or psychological warfare, with some officials suggesting the actions could be part of a broader strategy to disrupt travel. Flights from Ireland, Italy, the UK, Spain, and other countries were affected, with some flights rerouted or delayed due to the threats.

The incidents have led to significant disruption for passengers, with multiple flights diverted or grounded. Experts have noted the unusual nature of the threats, suggesting they may be part of a coordinated effort or a form of psychological warfare. Authorities in several countries have deployed bomb disposal teams and military fighter jets to respond to the threats, though no evidence of a hostile group or state actor has been found so far.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports at least 20 flights were affected, with one diverted to a military base in France, while The Guardian states at least 34 flights were impacted, including 25 on Thursday. The Guardian also mentions specific airlines and routes, such as Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, and Finnair, and notes that bomb threats were signed by "fighters of the Male State," a Russian far-right group. BBC and Al Jazeera report similar numbers but do not mention the "Male State" signature. NPR and Washington Examiner do not specify the number of flights or the signature of the threats, though NPR notes the threats followed other disruptions like cyber-attacks on refrigeration systems. Al Jazeera and The Guardian both mention a Ryanair flight from London to Sofia being diverted, while CBS and BBC do not specify the route of that flight.

Sources CBS News · The Guardian · BBC · Al Jazeera · NPR · Washington Examiner

Trump’s Economy Crushed Expectations Month Before Midterm Nightmare

The U.S. jobs market showed strong growth in October, with employers adding 165,000 jobs, surpassing expectations of 59,000. The unemployment rate dropped to 4.1%, below the predicted 4.2%. Revised figures for August and September increased the total job gains for those months by 84,000. The strongest gains were in professional and business services, healthcare, transportation and warehousing, and manufacturing. The report comes after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterms, which were heavily focused on economic issues. The Biden administration added 130,000 jobs to the federal workforce since taking office, while the Trump administration had cut over a million federal jobs. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% in October, with a 3.1% increase over the past year.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Fox Business both report that the Trump administration cut over a million federal jobs, while the Guardian and NPR do not mention this claim. The Daily Wire attributes the claim about cutting over a million jobs to Trump, while Fox Business does not attribute the claim. The Guardian and NPR do not mention the claim about cutting over a million jobs. The Daily Wire and Fox Business both report that the Biden administration added 130,000 jobs to the federal workforce, while the Guardian and NPR do not mention this. The Daily Wire and Fox Business both report that manufacturing jobs increased by 19,000 in October, while the Guardian and NPR do not mention this. The Daily Wire and Fox Business both report that the Trump administration reclassified about 8,000 senior federal positions to make it easier to fire employees, while the Guardian and NPR do not mention this.

Sources The Daily Wire · Newsweek · Straight Arrow News · Fox Business · NPR · The Guardian

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: A cult leader's 200-year sentence for killing 190 children marks a landmark legal reckoning with mass murder, directly impacting hundreds of families and reshaping criminal justice responses to cult violence.

Kenyan Cult Leader Sentenced to 200 Years for Killing 190 Children and One Adult

Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult, according to multiple outlets. The court found him guilty of ordering his followers to starve themselves and their children to death in the Shakahola Forest, with some victims also suffocated, strangled, or beaten. Mackenzie, founder of Good News International Church, was convicted alongside 28 others, including guards and gravediggers, for their roles in the killings. The sentences for Mackenzie include 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years for direct homicide, which will run consecutively. The court rejected the prosecution’s request for the death penalty, citing Kenya’s moratorium on executions since 1987. The case stems from the 2023 discovery of over 400 bodies in shallow graves at the Chakama Ranch in Shakahola, where Mackenzie’s followers lived in isolation.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after authorities received a tip about his activities. He had previously been arrested in 2017 on "radicalization" charges. The court found that Mackenzie’s teachings, which included fasting to meet Jesus, led to the deaths of his followers. Some victims were isolated and denied food while their parents watched, according to the judge. The court described the killings as "cold and calculated," with no remorse shown by the perpetrators. Mackenzie and his followers believed he was "Jesus’s mouthpiece," and those who resisted his orders were beaten to death.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Caller and CBS News report that Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years for killing 190 children and one adult, while The Guardian and BBC state he was convicted of murdering 191 people. The Guardian and BBC mention that 191 victims were identified, including 190 children and one adult, whereas The Daily Caller and CBS News refer to 190 children and one adult. The Guardian and BBC also note that 429 victims were identified by the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights, while The Daily Caller and CBS News mention 400 bodies exhumed. The Guardian and BBC report that Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after a tipoff, while The Daily Caller and CBS News state he was arrested in 2023 after a tip about his actions. The Guardian and BBC mention that Mackenzie was released on bail after his initial arrest, while The Daily Caller and CBS News do not specify this detail.

Sources The Daily Caller · The Daily Wire · BBC · Al Jazeera · CBS News · The Guardian
