Sources CBS News · Axios · The Hill · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · The Free Press

Judge rejects DOJ's push to force California to set aside ballots

A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration's bid to require California election officials to separate out mail ballots received from roughly 20,000 people it claims are not U.S. citizens. The decision from U.S. District Judge David Carter is the latest setback for the Trump administration in its efforts to exert more federal control over election administration just ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Carter said that the Justice Department's request for California to segregate and exclude more than 20,000 ballots violates "longstanding constitutional principles" giving states the authority to administer their own elections. The judge warned that requiring California election officials to set aside mail ballots received from those alleged noncitizens would likely lead to disenfranchisement.

The Trump administration sued California earlier this month as it alleged the state was sending 20,000 likely noncitizens ballots for the midterm contests. California has a universal mail-in voting program where all active voters are sent a ballot. Attorneys for California and Los Angeles County condemned the administration for not sharing who supplied its list. They argue they’re not required to prove voters’ citizenship merely because a sitting administration alleges issues, saying it’s not practical within the current timeline.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Hill both report that the Justice Department formed its list by checking a commercially-bought dataset with a government list of people who had been assigned numbers in the federal immigration system. Mother Jones and The Guardian add that the list was created by checking a commercially-bought dataset containing partial California voter rolls with a government list of people who had been assigned numbers in the federal immigration system. The Guardian also notes that the Department of Homeland Security identified up to 190,000 non-citizens on California voter rolls in July, but did not provide more details to the state until after ballots had already gone out. Al Jazeera reports that the Trump administration issued more than 100 subpoenas across 13 states as part of its search for alleged noncitizen voters. NPR states that the DOJ has charged dozens of people for registering or voting without being a U.S. citizen in the last two months.

Sources CBS News · The Hill · Mother Jones · The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera

Hegseth dismisses top military strategist from Joint Chiefs as Trump contemplates further Iran strikes

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the director for strategy, plans and policy, J5, from the Joint Staff this week. The move comes as President Donald Trump considers additional strikes on Iran following the upcoming midterm elections. The Pentagon has not publicly explained Sylvia’s dismissal, though some outlets report that a defense official accused him of leaking classified information related to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Sylvia’s departure follows a broader shakeup of the military’s top ranks, with him being the second general Hegseth has removed from that position in under a year. The administration has also warned Middle Eastern countries to prepare for potential escalation in the war with Iran. U.S. officials have told several countries to brace for possible American strikes after the midterms, along with possible Iranian retaliation. Trump has not made a final decision on military action but has suggested it could resume after the elections.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Straight Arrow News both report that Sylvia was removed from his position, but only Straight Arrow News attributes the dismissal to allegations of leaking classified information and failed polygraph tests. The Washington Examiner does not mention these allegations. The Daily Caller and Axios provide more detail on the alleged leaks, with Axios reporting that Sylvia admitted to leaking information to two reporters and failed multiple polygraph tests. The Intercept and The Free Press do not mention Sylvia’s dismissal or the alleged leaks, focusing instead on broader military and diplomatic developments in the region.

Sources Washington Examiner · Straight Arrow News · The Daily Caller · The Intercept · The Free Press · Axios

Obama and Trump spar at rallies in Georgia and Ohio: Key takeaways

Former US President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump held rival campaign rallies in Georgia and Ohio on Wednesday, trading criticism over the war in Iran, tariffs and the economy just five days before midterm elections. Obama criticized Trump’s handling of the Iran war, arguing it has made Americans less safe and increased the price of oil. He also took aim at Trump’s trade tariffs, claiming they have increased the cost of goods for American consumers. Trump, in turn, criticized Obama for letting the White House fall into disrepair and for not understanding cleanliness, while also accusing Obama of being involved in past political losses.

Obama again made fun of Trump’s White House renovations, comparing them to a Cheesecake Factory run by former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein. Trump responded by claiming he fixed up the White House “very inexpensively” and that the renovations were necessary to maintain the dignity of the executive mansion.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and New York Post both report Obama criticized Trump’s Iran war and the impact on oil prices, but Al Jazeera includes details about the ceasefire and the memorandum of understanding, which the New York Post omits. The New York Post mentions Trump’s claim that Obama “doesn’t understand cleanliness” and the White House renovations, which Al Jazeera does not include. The Washington Examiner and CBS News do not cover the Obama-Trump exchange in detail, focusing instead on other aspects of the midterms. The Daily Wire and Newsweek do not mention the rallies between Obama and Trump at all, focusing instead on other races and trends.

Sources Al Jazeera · CBS News · Washington Examiner · New York Post · Newsweek · The Daily Wire

Senate race in South Carolina tied in final stretch – poll

A new poll shows Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews tied with Republican incumbent Darline Graham at 48% each in South Carolina, making the race a dead heat. Graham, appointed to the seat after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died in July, entered the race with President Trump's endorsement. Trump returned to South Carolina to rally for Graham, attacking Andrews with anti-trans slurs and calling her a "radical left lunatic." Meanwhile, Andrews, a pediatrician, has focused her campaign on healthcare access and affordable prescriptions, while distancing herself from the Democratic party's left flank. The race is seen as a key contest in the Senate race, with Democrats hoping to flip the seat for the first time since 1998.

The Senate is still a toss-up with six states to decide the majority. On a good night for the Democrats, their ceiling rises to 54 seats. A good night for the Republicans could see them retain control with up to 52 seats. The outcome of the South Carolina race is seen as critical to the overall Senate balance, with both parties pouring significant resources into the state.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that South Carolina has moved from "Lean R" to "Toss-up" and that the Senate is still a toss-up with six states to decide the majority. NPR states that the Senate race is tight and that both parties have spent $40 million in the past month on the race. The Daily Caller notes that the Senate Leadership Fund spent $5 million on South Carolina in early October to help Graham. The Guardian and Axios do not mention the amount of money spent on the race. FOX News and The Guardian both mention that Graham is inexperienced and lacks national security expertise, while The Daily Caller adds that Graham stumbled during a debate on national security issues.

Sources FOX News · NPR · Axios · Newsweek · The Guardian · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Brewers End Historic Drought, Defeat Rays For First World Series Title

The Milwaukee Brewers secured their first World Series title by defeating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on October 28. The victory ended a 56-year championship drought for the Brewers, who had previously reached the World Series only once in 1982. The Rays, seeking their first title, fell short after a thrilling 12-inning Game 4 win. The Brewers' dominant postseason run included 11 wins and two losses, with standout performances from rookie Cooper Pratt and Jacob Misiorowski, who pitched five scoreless innings before leaving due to a calf injury. Trevor Megill closed the game with a save, and the Brewers' bullpen was nearly unhittable, posting a 1.38 ERA and 0.86 WHIP in 13 playoff games.

The Brewers' victory was marked by strong offensive output, with Pratt and Jackson Chourio each batting over .400 in the series. Pratt contributed seven RBIs, while the Rays managed only 11 RBIs as a team. The Rays' ace, Drew Rasmussen, allowed just one run in four innings but struggled against the Brewers' bullpen, which extended the lead to 4-0 after six innings. The Rays' players watched in stunned silence from the dugout as the Brewers celebrated in the middle of Tropicana Field, awaiting their own parade for the first time in their 28-year history.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek reports that the Rays fell short on both sides of the ball, while The Guardian and BBC attribute the Rays' failure to their inability to capitalize on opportunities, such as a fourth-inning error by Sal Frelick. NPR and ABC News mention the Rays' 12-inning Game 4 win, while CBS News refers to it as a "dramatic come-from-behind 4-3 victory in the 12th inning of Game Four." The Guardian and BBC provide more detail on William Contreras' MVP performance, including his .381/.435/.429 line and his role in containing Tampa Bay's running game, which is not explicitly mentioned in Newsweek or CBS News. The Guardian and BBC also note Contreras' World Baseball Classic win with Venezuela, which is omitted in other accounts.

Sources Newsweek · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · CBS News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Democrats Want Me In Jail For A Post Explaining Election Security

The Federalist article details a post by the author on X, where they discussed election security measures, specifically referencing President Trump's 2019 executive order under the National Emergencies Act. The author claims that the post led to calls for their prosecution by Marc Elias and Stuart Stevens, who suggested RICO charges. The author argues that their post was about implementing a mitigation plan outlined by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to secure voting machines, not about seizing them. The post was included in a Media Matters article titled “Election Denial Movement Sets Stage for Chaos on Election Day and its Aftermath.”

ABC News reports that James O'Keefe and Cam Higby face charges in Minnesota for posting undercover videos that allegedly involved misrepresenting their identities to test election security. The charges include unlawful voting and identity theft. O'Keefe and Higby claim the videos were meant to expose vulnerabilities in the voting system, not to commit fraud. O'Keefe called the charges "weaponized lawfare" and defended the videos as journalism.

Newsweek states that O'Keefe and Higby were charged with unlawful voting and identity theft after they allegedly used the names of registered voters without permission during a test of Minnesota’s voter-vouching process. The charges focus on their alleged conduct while applying for ballots, which included not signing the required oath. Minnesota’s vouching process allows a registered voter to confirm the identity of up to eight additional voters, but the process does not permit using another voter's identity.

Where the accounts differ

The Federalist attributes the call for prosecution to Marc Elias and Stuart Stevens, while ABC News and Newsweek focus on the charges against O'Keefe and Higby. The Federalist mentions a post on X and a Media Matters article, which are not referenced in ABC News or Newsweek. The Federalist claims the author was not accused of seizing voting machines, while ABC News and Newsweek do not mention this claim. The Federalist also references a 2019 executive order and DHS mitigation plans, which are not covered in the other accounts.

Sources The Federalist · ABC News · Newsweek · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Three killed in midair helicopter collision near Oregon airport, authorities confirm

Two helicopters collided midair near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon on Thursday afternoon, resulting in the deaths of all three occupants, according to multiple outlets. The collision occurred around 2:15 p.m. local time, involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus H125. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed the incident, and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is leading the investigation. The crash site was near Oregon Route 233, approximately one mile west of Dayton, with nearby roads closed for emergency response. The airport remained open, though operations were not disrupted.

The victims included 22-year-old Texas flight instructor Maddie Aasbo, a British student pilot, and 38-year-old Oregon pilot Tyler Delane Sturdevant. The British student pilot's identity has not been publicly released, pending notification of next of kin. One of the helicopters was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, an aviation school based at the airport, which expressed condolences and stated it was cooperating with authorities.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and CBS News differ on the number of occupants in each helicopter. FOX News states the Robinson R22 had two people and the Airbus H125 had one, while CBS News reports the opposite, stating the Robinson R22 had one occupant and the Airbus H125 had two. New York Post and Newsweek both report the Robinson R22 had two people and the Airbus H125 had one, but Newsweek adds that the Airbus was a 2018 model, while FOX News and CBS News do not specify the model of the Airbus. BBC does not mention the model of either helicopter. Additionally, Newsweek and BBC provide more detail on the crash location, specifying it was in a farm field, while FOX News and CBS News refer to it as a field off Oregon Route 233.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · CBS News · Newsweek · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Federal judge blocks Trump’s Medicaid rule, protecting millions from being denied coverage based on outdated medical criteria.

US judge blocks Trump’s Medicaid rule forcing ill to prove impairment

A federal judge ruled against enforcing a new rule by the Trump administration that would require chronically ill people on Medicaid to prove themselves “medically frail” to qualify for work exemptions. US District Judge Richard Stearns blocked the rule, siding with 25 states and the District of Columbia, which had sued the administration in June over the change. The states argued the rule unlawfully limits exemptions for people with serious medical conditions. The law defines “medically frail” to include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. The administration’s rule required people in those categories to show their conditions also “significantly impair” their ability to comply with work requirements. The plaintiffs argued the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need and overstep the law’s text.

Starting January 1, 2027, Medicaid expansion enrollees aged 19 to 63 must show they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. Exceptions include those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs. While the ruling makes it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, it does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful. Stearns, who serves in the District of Massachusetts and was appointed by President Bill Clinton, upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty that the states and the District of Columbia had contested.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera states the rule requires people in certain categories to show their conditions “significantly impair” their ability to comply with work requirements, while Washington Examiner does not mention this specific requirement. Al Jazeera also notes that the ruling does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful, whereas Washington Examiner does not explicitly state this. Al Jazeera mentions that the law defines “medically frail” to include people with certain disabilities that “significantly impair” daily activities, while Washington Examiner does not include this detail.

Sources Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Record Turnout, Suspected Fraud: Israel’s Election Day

Israel held its 26th Knesset elections on Tuesday, with historic voter turnout reported. The Central Elections Committee noted that by 2:00 p.m., turnout had reached 44.9%, the highest in the initial seven hours since 1969. Turnout among Israeli Defense Forces members reached 48% by 1:00 p.m. The election was marked by a high-profile voter fraud investigation in the Negev, where three residents of Bedouin communities were arrested on suspicion of planning to buy votes for Ra’am (The United Arab List party). Police seized envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with notes and ballot slips, and the suspects were set to appear in court on Tuesday.

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, faced a serious challenge from former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, whose newly formed Yashar Party surged in recent polls. Exit polls suggested that the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition. However, the final results remain uncertain, with neither bloc securing a majority in the 120-seat parliament. The election is seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership, particularly in light of the October 7 intelligence failures and ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that police seized envelopes containing Ra’am ballots, with cash found in some of them, while The Guardian and NPR do not mention this detail. The Guardian and NPR describe exit polls suggesting the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot would win most seats, while The Daily Wire and Axios note that Netanyahu’s Likud Party emerged as the largest party. The Guardian and CBS News mention that Netanyahu’s Likud Party has 20.8% of the vote with 85% of votes counted, while The Daily Wire and Axios report different seat projections. The Guardian and CBS News also note that Arab parties are projected to win 19 seats, a record, while The Daily Wire and Axios do not specify the number of seats for Arab parties. The Daily Wire and Axios mention that the final parliamentary distributions will hinge on late-tally ballots cast by security personnel and citizens unable to access standard stations, while The Guardian and CBS News do not include this detail.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · CBS News · Axios

Trump accuses Democrats of election fraud in Alaska Senate race

President Donald Trump accused Democrats and Mary Peltola's campaign of fraud and perjury after the New York Times reported that Peltola aides helped recruit another candidate named Dan Sullivan. The report described a "ballot composition project" involving Peltola campaign staff, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) officials, political consultants, and an operative who traveled through Alaska using a false name to recruit potential candidates. The DOJ is seeking to delay certification of the election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, citing possible voter confusion between two candidates with nearly identical names. Peltola's campaign denied involvement in the second Sullivan's candidacy, stating they have no connection to either Sullivan campaign.

The Department of Justice is facing a legal battle in Alaska, where it is trying to convince a federal court that confusion between two Senate candidates with nearly identical names could be enough to delay certification of the election results. The DOJ's complaint stems from a controversy in Alaska where two individuals by the name of Dan Sullivan, one a retired schoolteacher and the other the state’s incumbent senator, appear alongside each other on the state’s ballots. The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides worked with a veteran Democratic operative named Jerid Kurtz to recruit another Dan Sullivan to run for Alaska’s Senate seat, hoping voter confusion would draw support from the incumbent Republican senator.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that Trump is organizing a cross-country campaign blitz and has spent $277 million since Sept. 1 to help Republicans, while The Hill notes that more than 50,000 ballots have already been cast in the state. The Daily Wire and Axios both describe Trump's accusations of perjury and fraud, but only Axios mentions that Trump offered no evidence to support his claims. FOX News and The Hill both note that the DOJ is seeking to delay certification of the election results, but only FOX News states that the DOJ is conducting an "aggressive criminal investigation" into how the second Sullivan secured a spot on Alaska's ballot.

Sources ABC News · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · FOX News · Axios · The Hill

Trump’s Visa Crackdown Has an Exception: His Friends

Flavio Bolsonaro, the defeated right-wing Brazilian presidential candidate and Donald Trump ally, and his family received U.S. visas to enter the country. The Trump administration continues to implement widespread visa restrictions while suspending and revoking existing ones. Bolsonaro and his family arrived in the U.S. on Wednesday, having entered Argentina from Brazil and then flown to Ecuador before landing in Miami. They were shielded from photographers by umbrellas as they left the airport. Bolsonaro, who lost the presidential election to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, has refused to concede and claims there was election fraud. The State Department confirmed it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, though the administration has not commented further on the matter.

Bolsonaro faces multiple investigations in Brazil, including allegations of money laundering and tax evasion. Brazilian authorities ordered him to surrender his passports by Tuesday, but he reportedly left the country before complying. The Trump administration has supported Bolsonaro and his family, with Trump calling the election results "rigged" and expressing concern over Brazil’s judicial system. Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo, has been living in the U.S. since early 2025, acting as a key link between the Brazilian far right and Trump’s circle.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and NPR both state that Bolsonaro and his family entered Argentina before flying to Ecuador and then to Miami, while ABC News and FOX News report that Bolsonaro arrived directly in Miami. NPR and Mother Jones mention that Bolsonaro’s family was escorted by uniformed officers with umbrellas, a detail not included in ABC News or FOX News. Mother Jones and NPR note that Bolsonaro claimed the election was fraudulent and that he was not fleeing but leaving a "state of exception," a claim not explicitly made by ABC News or FOX News. FOX News reports that Bolsonaro’s departure was confirmed by an ally, while Mother Jones and NPR do not attribute this claim to a specific source. ABC News states that Brazilian authorities were unaware of Bolsonaro’s flight, while Mother Jones and NPR do not mention this.

Sources Mother Jones · ABC News · FOX News · NPR · Axios · Washington Examiner

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded United Farm Workers, dies at 96

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers, has died at 96, according to her family. The New York Times reported that the cause of death was cancer. Huerta, along with Cesar Chavez, founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, which later became the United Farm Workers. The union helped secure labor contracts and better conditions for agricultural workers, including the right to unionize in California. Huerta was a key organizer, coordinating boycotts and negotiations. She also popularized the slogan “Sí, se puede,” which later became a rallying cry for Democrats. In March, she publicly spoke of being raped by Chavez in the 1960s, which resulted in two pregnancies. She said she kept the secret to protect the movement. Huerta continued to work as an activist, lobbying for immigration reform and supporting civil rights causes.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News and The Daily Wire both report that Huerta said Chavez raped her in 1966, but The Daily Wire adds that she had two pregnancies and that the children were raised by others. Straight Arrow News does not mention the pregnancies or the children. The Guardian and Mother Jones do not mention the allegations against Chavez, focusing instead on Huerta’s activism and legacy. The Daily Wire states that Huerta kept her account of abuse secret for six decades, while Straight Arrow News says she first spoke of the allegations in March. The Guardian and Mother Jones do not mention the allegations against Chavez, focusing instead on Huerta’s activism and legacy. The Daily Wire and Straight Arrow News both mention that Huerta said she wasn’t aware of Chavez abusing underage girls, but The Daily Wire adds that the Times investigation indicated other victims existed.

Sources Straight Arrow News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Mother Jones · ABC News · Axios

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Two high-speed trains collide in Spain, killing at least 64

Two high-speed trains collided in Spain on Wednesday, resulting in at least 64 deaths and 80 injuries. The crash occurred near Toledo, with witnesses reporting passengers being thrown into the air. The trains were traveling from Madrid to Seville when one struck the rear of a stationary train. Spain’s transport minister attributed the crash to an “inexplicable” decision by a train controller, while the prime minister vowed to investigate and hold those responsible accountable. The incident marks the second major high-speed rail disaster in Spain this year, following a similar crash in January that killed over 40 people.

Spain’s high-speed rail system, once considered the most advanced in Europe, has faced renewed scrutiny following the collision. The crash occurred on a section of track where a computer malfunction caused a signal fault, leading to the stopping of multiple trains. According to officials, an order was given to resume traffic despite an active stop signal, contributing to the collision. Rescue efforts continued through the night, with teams searching for survivors and recovering bodies from the wreckage.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News and The Guardian both report the death toll as at least 64, while The Daily Caller and The Hill state at least 68. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention the January crash killed 45 people, while Straight Arrow News and The Hill report 40. The Daily Caller and The Guardian attribute the crash to a signal fault, while The Daily Wire and The Hill cite a computer malfunction. The Daily Caller and The Guardian report the collision occurred near Toledo, while The Hill and The Guardian specify the location as between Urda and Los Yebenes. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention the transport minister called the crash “inexplicable,” while Straight Arrow News and The Hill attribute the crash to an “inexplicable” decision by a train controller.

Sources Straight Arrow News · The Daily Caller · Al Jazeera · The Hill · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Judge denies the Justice Department's bid to stop processing California ballots

A federal judge has denied the Department of Justice's request to segregate thousands of California ballots in the midterm elections. The DOJ sought to stop processing ballots for 20,000 individuals it claims are "likely" noncitizens. California officials argued that the DOJ's list is unreliable and that segregating ballots days before Election Day would be unlawful and disenfranchise voters. The judge emphasized that once ballots are segregated, lasting harm occurs and that the DOJ's actions could threaten democracy.

The judge ruled that the DOJ failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on its claims and that the requested relief could disrupt the election. He also noted that the DOJ has filed numerous lawsuits seeking voter rolls without success. The ruling cited concerns about inaccuracies in citizenship databases and the potential for false positives. The judge warned that changing election procedures close to an election could create confusion and disenfranchise lawful voters.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and Newsweek both state that the DOJ requested a temporary restraining order to segregate ballots, while Washington Examiner and ABC News mention the judge's intention to appoint a special master to probe the DOJ's process. Al Jazeera and Straight Arrow News report that the DOJ's request was part of a broader effort across multiple states, including Washington. NPR and Newsweek note that the DOJ has charged dozens of people for illegally voting as noncitizens, while ABC News and Al Jazeera mention the Trump administration's broader subpoena efforts. Straight Arrow News adds that the DOJ's request was part of a larger pattern of subpoenas in 13 states, which other accounts do not mention.

Sources NPR · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · ABC News · Straight Arrow News · Al Jazeera

No source labeled right covered this story.

UN holds annual vote on condemning US embargo on Cuba as tensions spill into public

The United Nations is set to vote Wednesday on a resolution condemning the decades-long U.S. economic embargo on Cuba as tensions between the two nations escalate. The vote, which has occurred annually for 34 years, is expected to pass with overwhelming support from the 193 member states. The resolution reflects global opinion on the U.S. policy, though it is not legally binding. The vote comes amid Cuba's deepening financial crisis and the Trump administration's intensified campaign against the island, including threats of military intervention. On Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez engaged in a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly. Rodríguez accused Waltz of lying, prompting Waltz to demand he "back up" and reminded him he was in the U.N., not the White House. The confrontation followed a similar incident the previous week when Waltz and Cuban delegate Ernesto Soberón Guzmán clashed outside a U.S.-hosted panel.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that the U.S. embargo was first imposed in 1960 after Fidel Castro's revolution, while the New York Post and FOX News do not mention the historical context of the embargo. The New York Post and The Daily Wire describe Waltz showing images of Fidel Castro wearing Rolex watches and displaying photos of Cuban elites' luxury properties, which are not mentioned in ABC News or BBC. The Newsweek account states that Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed paperwork to expel a Cuban diplomat, a detail absent in the other accounts. The Daily Wire and Newsweek attribute the expulsion to Rubio, while ABC News and FOX News do not mention any expulsion. The BBC account omits details about the embargo's history, the luxury properties, and the expulsion, focusing only on the shouting match.

Sources ABC News · New York Post · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Newsweek · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

US central bank holds interest rates steady ahead of midterm elections – here's what that means

The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at its final monetary policy meeting before the midterm elections, with 10 of 12 committee members voting to keep the federal funds rate at 3.75%-4%. The decision followed a September rate hike and came amid elevated inflation. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh stated the central bank aims to gather more information before making further decisions. The Fed uses interest rate changes to manage inflation and stabilize the job market. Leaving rates unchanged means borrowing costs for mortgages, business loans, and savings remain stable.

The Fed acknowledged that inflation remains high but noted signs of economic resilience. Policymakers emphasized the need for more data before adjusting rates again. The next meeting is scheduled for December 8-9. While the decision was not unanimous, two members—Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Fed Governor Lisa Cook—voted to increase rates to 4%-4.25%. The Fed's next meeting will be held over 8-9 December.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the Fed's decision was not unanimous, with 10 of 12 members voting to keep rates unchanged, while Cook and Hammack voted to increase rates. The Daily Caller states that the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points in September, which was the first increase since 2023, and that the CPI increased 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the preceding 12 months. Fox Business notes that the Fed raised rates by 25 basis points in September, which was the first increase since July 2023. The Daily Wire mentions that the Fed had raised rates for the first time in three years in September and that the probability of another rate hike was 7.2% according to CME Group’s FedWatch. ABC News states that the Fed raised rates a quarter of a percentage point last month, marking the first rate increase in three years, and that prices increased 3.7% in September compared to a year earlier. Straight Arrow News reports that the Fed's benchmark interest rate was unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, following a quarter-point increase in September, which was the Fed’s first rate hike in three years.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Fox Business · ABC News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: A fire at a South Carolina nuclear site poses immediate risks of radiation leaks, endangering public health and safety for thousands.

Emergency declared at South Carolina nuclear site after lab fire

A fire broke out at the Savannah River National Laboratory near Aiken, South Carolina, prompting an emergency declaration. The incident occurred around 5:39 p.m. Eastern Time, according to multiple accounts. The fire was extinguished by 9:45 p.m., and officials stated that no contamination was detected outside the facility. The Savannah River Site (SRS) declared a Site Area Emergency and later terminated it after radiological surveys found no detectable levels of contamination. One employee was reported to have suffered minor injuries and was taken to a hospital.

The fire led to temporary restrictions on rail, river, and air traffic near the site, as well as the closure of site entrances. Highway 125 remained open, and protective actions were lifted by 9:45 p.m. SRS officials coordinated with state and local agencies during the incident. Residents were advised to monitor local media for updates.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Just The News both state that the fire was reported at 5:39 p.m., while the New York Post and Newsweek mention 5:40 p.m. and 5:07 p.m., respectively. The New York Post and Newsweek report that the emergency was declared at 5:07 p.m. and 5:39 p.m., respectively, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not specify the exact time of the emergency declaration. The New York Post and Newsweek mention that the fire caused an “unfiltered ground-level radiological release,” while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not include this detail. The New York Post and Newsweek attribute the statement about no contamination outside the facility to the Department of Energy spokesperson, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News attribute it to SRS officials.

Sources Washington Examiner · Just The News · FOX News · New York Post · Newsweek

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.
